HEADNOTE: Section 4, read with section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Valuation of excisable goods - Valuation: Packing - Gas Cylinder detention charges excludible--handling etc. upto factory gate includible. Recoveries in excess of actual Post Manufacturing Expenses includible. Limitation (Extended) applicable as handling charges not included

FACT: The appellants manufacture industrial gases, in their price list given to the Department they did not include handling charges (loading, unloading, transport etc.) and cylinder detention charges. These were recovered from customers by issuing debit notes and this was not declared before the authorities. After show cause proceedings, the Collector of Central Excise ordered that Rs. 10,15,798.19 ps. was to be paid by the petitioner for the period April, 1979 to February, 1984. A penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 was also imposed. Department also argued that the amount recovered as handling charges was far in excess of actual expenses incurred.

HELD: Limitation--extended 5 year period is applicable because as per the Rules, the appellants should have included handling and other charges upto factory gate in their price list. Hence penalty is also justified. "Filing of price lists is a statutory requirement. Accordingly we hold that there was suppression of facts on the part of the appellants and the extended period of limitation in terms of provisions of sub-section (1) of Section 11A of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 is applicable in this case. Consequently penalty on the appellants is also justified but in view of the fact that in succeeding paragraphs we are allowing deduction of some of the elements, we consider it fair to reduce the penalty to Rs. 50,000/- (Rupees fifty thousand only)."

2. Cylinder detention or rental being post-manufacturing expenses are not includible in assessable value. "...we hold that cylinder detention charges recovered by the appellants are not includible in the assessable value."

3. Handling and loading charges upto factory gate from part of assessable value, but similar expenses outside factory gate are not. "The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Assistant Collector of Central Excise and Others v. Madras Rubber Factory and Others reported in 1987 (27) ELT 553, 1987 (10) ECR--625 had held that the cost of distribution is not includible in case the whole-sale dealers take delivery of the goods from the outside duty-paid godowns. Accordingly the findings by the Collector that the handling charges incurred after the factory gate stage and recovered by the appellants are includible are set aside. However, the handling charges, if any incurred upto the factory gate stage would be includible in the assessable value.

4. Remand--Amount recovered in outside factory gate transactions, which are in excess of actual expenses incurred to be taken as part of the price realised by the appellant. Issue remanded for re-adjudication in the light of the above findings. "During the course of arguments the learned Jt. C.D.R. had argued that the amounts recovered from the customers under various heads were far in excess of the expenses actually incurred by the appellants on handling and unloading charges. We hold that the expenses actually incurred by the appellants on permissible deductions alone would be excludible and any excess recoveries from customers would be considered as part of the appellant's price realisation."

On appeal : HELD: From the case records, it was found that the assessee had collected various charges from importers/exporters including passengers for keeping the cargo in transit safely, pending export or customs clearance for home consumption. In holding that keeping safe custody of cargo in transit, pending clearance by the customs would constitute an activity exigible under the above entry, the lower authorities had relied on Circulars of the CBEC which clarified that storage and warehousing service provided by, inter alia, Airport Authority is covered by the entry. The entry cargo handling service was clarified by the CBEC as not covering export cargo and passenger baggage. The clarification was not to the effect that all activities relating to export cargo and passenger baggage were also excluded from levy under other entries. The finding of the Commissioner, that the exceptions provided under cargo handling services with regard to passenger baggage and export cargo could not be claimed under storage and warehousing services, was to be agreed with. [Para 9.2]

Demurrage or wharfage charges were collected, respectively, in relation to clearance of import/export cargo beyond five days and 24 hours. As found by the original authority, these were higher charges for continued storage of cargo collected by the assessee from members of the trade. These were part of the taxable value collected towards storage and warehouse charges. [Para 9.3]

As regards the abandoned cargo, those accrued to the assessee towards storage and warehousing of cargo, which were not taken delivery of by the importer. The procedure for auctioning abandoned cargo and the sharing of the proceeds is prescribed by the Ministry of Finance. These instructions also make it clear that the assessee would receive amounts towards the service of storage and warehousing of cargo under this head. However, the services were not rendered to any person in the case of the abandoned cargo. Therefore, demand under this head was not sustainable. [Para 9.4]

As regards the destination charges, it was found that the assessee had collected the documents representing the consignments brought by Air India and Blue Dart and hand over these to the respective consignees. In cases where the assessee merely collected and handed over the documents to the respective consignees, destination charges would not form part of taxable value under storage and warehousing. [Para 9.5]

As regards the OT charges/penalties, the lower authorities had not given a finding as to the nature and purpose of these penalties but had presumed that these were collected for violations on the part of their clients in relation to storage and warehousing services. The Commissioner (Appeals) did not find this item to be taxable under storage and warehousing. In the absence of a finding as to how that amount was taxable towards any service rendered by the assessee, it was difficult to accept the stand of the revenue in this regard. The assessee had also not explained the nature and purpose of collecting these charges. This matter would be decided after hearing the party afresh. [Para 9.6]

Considering the nature of the activities involved, the Commissioner could not have found with certainty that the assessee had deliberately mis-classified the activities undertaken by it under the head ‘Cargo handling services’ instead of ‘Storage and warehousing services’. Therefore, the authorities could not have validly invoked extended period and imposed penalties. The penal liability of the assessee required reconsideration in the light of section 80. [Para 9.7]

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Valuation of goods for excise - Valuation - Loading/unloading outside factory gate not includible as per S.C. judgment in Indian Oxygen Ltd. case. CESA: S. 4. Limitation--Suppression--Charges realised through separate bills not declared; extended limitation applicable. CESA: S. 11A. Dissented

FACT: By review order under Section 35(b) CESA, the Collector added Rs. 9472.95 to the assessable value of the appellants who are manufacturers of metal containers, on the ground that they charged from customers freight at a higher rate than declared. Longer period of limitation was also invoked.

HELD: I Minority view per Member (J)]: Valuation--Unloading charges outside factory gate are not includible in the assessable value. As regards loading charges within the factory, there is no specific charge in the show cause notice. It refers to freight, which is also not includible in the assessable value. (Ratio of Indian Oxygen Ltd. v. CCE Bombay Tyre International). "There is no specific charge that they have charged loading/unloading charges at higher rates than declared. It is only the Collector who says that the appellants charged loading and unloading charges at a particular rate. According to the decision of the Supreme Court........unloading charges outside the factory-gate are not includible in the assessable value. Therefore, the question of mis-declaration as regards the inclusion of unloading charges outside the factory-gate falls to the ground. As regards the inclusion of loading charges within the factory-gate, the charge in this show cause is vague. It refers to freight. According to Bombay Tyre International..........freight is not includible in the assessable value. According to the language used in the show cause notice, the entire charge of charging freight at a higher rate falls to the ground in view of the Bombay Tyre International However, taking into account the order of the Collector, the loading within the factory is includible. As stated earlier, there is no specific allegation to this effect in the show cause notice."

Limitation--Before the judgment of the Supreme Court in Indian Oxygen case (1988) the question of includibility of loading charges incurred within the factory was not clear and the law was in a fluid state. As such, the charge of misdeclaration when the legal position itself is not clear is like charging the appellants in vacuum. The show cause notice is, therefore, barred by limitation. "Till the judgment of the Supreme Court in the Indian Oxygen case, the decision as to the includibility of loading charges within the factory is not clear and law was in a fluid state. In Bombay Tyre International, it is not specifically stated that loading charges within the factory is to be included although it was categorically observed that the expenses incurred upto the factory-gate cannot be deducted from the assessable value. Therefore, to charge the manufacturer with mis-declaration when legal position itself is not clear is like charging him in vacuum. Therefore, we are of the view that the show cause notice is barred by limitation. Accordingly, we allow the appeal and set aside the order of the lower authority on grounds that the show cause notice is barred by limitation. The appeal is, thus, allowed."

[Majority view per Member (T) Vice-President]: Valuation--The appellants admittedly collected transportation charges, be it for loading, unloading or handling the barrels. Of these, the charges incurred on loading and handling of goods within the factory are required to be included in the assessable value, according to the Supreme Court's judgment in Indian Oxygen Ltd For determining such charges, the case is remanded to the Asstt. Collector. There is thus an admission on the part of the appellants that the so-called transportation charges 'or delivery charges', whatever the name was given to them by the appellants included some charges towards loading within the factory on the wagons, trucks, etc from the stacking place after the manufacture of barrels and metal containers. This being the position and in view of the Supreme Court's judgment in the case of Indian Oxygen Ltd. v. CCE. expenses incurred towards the loading of the goods within the factory are required to be included in the assessable value of the goods Since a separate break-up of these charges is not given out of the total transportation cost or delivery charges collected by the assessee from its customers, the case has necessarily to be remanded for determining the charges collected towards loading and handling of the goods within the factory for the purpose of charging duty thereon and I order accordingly."

accepted the contentions of the assessee so far as ocean freight of Rs. 49.39 lakhs paid by the assessee to these Indian agents of non-resident shipping companies towards the ocean freight while rest of the amount of Rs. 9.60 lakhs paid towards other service charges were disallowed by the Commissioner (Appeals) by invoking provision of section 40(a)(ia) as assessee had not deducted tax at source on such payments..

On appeal to the Tribunal: HELD: The non-resident shipping companies have confirmed vide freight certificates to have received the same amount of other service charges which are mainly terminal handling charges, documentation charges, demurrage etc. from these agents. It is observed that provision of section 172(8) also stipulate that other charges such as demurrage or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature are also covered by provision of section 172(2) by virtue of provisions of section 172(8), which by virtue of CBDT Circular No 723, dated 19-9-1995 shall also take it out of provision of section 194C for deduction of tax at source. As discussed, the non-resident shipping companies have given two freight certificates with respect to each bill raised by BS Corporation, the first pertain to ocean freight which is already accepted by Commissioner (Appeals) while granting relief to the assessee and revenue is not in appeal against relief granted by the Commissioner (Appeals), and the second freight certificate is with respect to THC charges and documentation charges which are acknowledged to be received by non-resident shipping companies, thus it leaves no doubt that these are merely reimbursement of expenses as also claimed by BS Corporation vide debit note and are in the nature of payment referred to in section 172(8) and hence are covered by provision of section 172(2) and no income tax was required to be deducted at source under section 194C keeping in view special provisions relating to taxability of non-resident shipping companies who have to discharge their liabilities towards income tax before leaving port or to make satisfactory arrangements for payment of taxes as are contained in section 172 and section 44B. HEADNOTE: Section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 - Levy of additional duty - Additional duty (CVD) of customs is calculated on the aggregate of CIF value plus basic duty and any other customs duty

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Additional duty of customs (CVD) is not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India--Value for assessment is the landed cost including charges upto point of clearance

Section 25 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Exemption from Customs duty - Exemption notification can be availed of only where its conditions are satisfied--Notification 302/79-CE

FACT: The petitioners imported in February 1983, 51 metric tonnes of High Density Polyethylene Moulding Powder. Customs duty and auxiliary duty was levied on the item at the rate of 50% and 25% respectively of the c.i.f. value and the additional or countervailing duty was fixed at the rate of 42% of c.i.f. value added on to customs duty. The petitioners contended that loading of customs duty on c.i.f. value for the purpose of arriving at countervailing duty is not permissible; that there should be partial exemption of countervailing duty as prescribed by Notification No. 302/79-CE and that landing and port charges were not to be added on the dutiable value of the imported item.

HELD: Additional duty (CVD) duty--Customs duty to be added on to c.i.f. value while determining countervailing duty. "The sub-section opens with the words for the purpose of calculating under Section 3 the additional duty on any imported article....'. It further recites that the value of the imported article shall be the aggregate of (a) the value of the imported article determined under sub-section (1) of Section 14, and (b) any duty of customs chargeable on that article under Section 12 of the Customs Act. In view of the clear statutory provision, it is futile for Dr. Kantawala to submit that the customs duty cannot be loaded on c.i.f. value while determining assessable value for the purpose of additional or countervailing duty." [Section 3(2) of Customs Tariff Act, 1975].

2. Value of imported goods not determined at point of entry--all expenses till goods are cleared from port form part of the value of imported goods. "In our judgment, the taxable event continues till the goods are cleared at Customs barrier for home consumption and all the expenses which are required to be incurred in respect of those imported goods form part of the value of those goods and it is not permissible for the importer to suggest that the value of goods should be determined at the point of time of entry into territorial waters and all expenses incurred thereafter are post-import expenses."

3. Exemption Notification No. 302/79-CE--its impact on countervailing duty--advantage of Notification available only after fulfilling both conditions of the said notification. "The advantage of the notification dated December 4, 1979 is available provided both the conditions are satisfied, the conditions being that the goods are manufactured from raw naphtha and on which the appropriate amount of excise duty has already been paid. It is obvious that the imported goods cannot satisfy the second condition, because the payment of excise duty on raw naphtha can never arise in respect of imported goods." [Notification No. 302/79-CE; CE Rule 8(i)]

4. Additional Duty (CVD): Duties imposed under Section 3(2) of CTA are neither void nor unconstitutional. "It is impossible to accede to the submission of the learned counsel. The two categories of tax-payers cannot be bracketed in the same class and it would be improper to suggest that the goods locally manufactured and the goods imported form the same class. In our judgment, the two categories of goods are not at all comparable and totally distinct and different. Levy of countervailing duty on the value ascertained by addition of customs duty to c.i.f. value cannot be claimed to be discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. .....In our judgment, the Section does not suffer from any vice and cannot be struck down."

Section 11AB deals with 'Interest on delayed payment of duty'. [Para 13]

Rule 4 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 deals with 'Duty payable on removal'.

Rule 5 deals with 'Date of determination of duty and tariff valuation'.

Rule 6 deals with 'Assessment of duty'.

Rule 7 deals with 'Provisional assessment'.

Rule 8 deals with 'Manner of payment'. [Para 14] Excise duty is a duty on manufacture or production of goods. It is, however, collected at the point of removal of goods. When the duty of excise is chargeable with reference to the value of goods, section 4 provides that on each removal of the goods, the value will be determined either under clause (a) or clause (b).

Section 4 yields the following elements:

(i)

when the goods are sold;

(ii)

for delivery;

(iii)

at the time and place of removal;

(iv)

the assessee and the buyer not being related;

(v)

price is the sole consideration for the sale, then the transaction value will be the value for the determination of excise duty.

The price may be what is actually paid or what is payable for the goods when sold.

Apart from what is shown as the price the transaction value would include:

(i)

Any amount the buyer is liable to pay to the assessee by reason of or in connection with the sale whether at the time of the sale or any other time.

(ii)

Any amount payable on behalf of the assessee by reason of or in connection with the sale whether at the time of sale or any other time.

(iii)

The aforesaid amounts encompass certain amounts which are specifically enumerated, namely, advertising, publicity, marketing and selling, organizational expenses, storage, outward handling serving, warranty, commission or any other matter. [Para 15]

Thus the intent is to determine the value by not only including the actual price paid or payable but all amounts which are separately enumerated. [Para 16]

Rule 4 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 falls under the heading 'duty payable on removal'. It is contemplated that duty is to be paid on the goods in the manner provided under rule 8 or under any law. No excisable good on which duty is payable can be removed without payment of excise duty unless otherwise provided. Rule 8 under the heading 'manner of payment' declares that duty on the goods removed from the factory, etc. during a month shall be paid by the 5th day of the following month. Removal, however, in the month of March will entail liability to pay by 31st day of March. Sub-rule (3) of rule 8 provides for liability with the assessee who fails to pay the amount by the due date. Sub-rule (4) refers to liability to pay interest. It is amply clear that the expression 'due date' would be 5th day of the month following the month during which the goods are removed except with regard to the goods removed during the month of March in which case the due date would be 31st day of March. [Para 17]

The Scheme of the Rules further is that assessment is to be done by the assessee itself by way of self-assessment and the duty paid by the due date. What is to happen when the assessee is confronted with a situation when it is unable to determine the value of the goods or find the rate of duty. Rule 7 provides the solution. The assessee can thereunder apply giving reasons and seeking permission to make a provisional assessment. The Officer may grant such permission. Thereupon duty is payable on a provisional basis. The value or the rate would be indicated by the Officer in the order permitting such provisional assessment. This is, however, made subject to the assessee executing a bond binding the assessee to pay the difference between the duty as payable under the final assessment and the provisional assessment. The final assessment is to be made within six months from the date of communication of the order permitting provisional assessment under rule 7(1). The period can be extended by the Commissioner for six months and by the Chief Commissioner for which there is no time limit.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 7 provides as follows:

(1)

The assessee shall be liable to pay interest.

(2)

On any amount payable based on a final assessment under rule 7(3).

(3)

At the rate fixed under section 11A or section 11B of the Act.

(4)

From the first date of the month succeeding the month for which the amount is determined till the date of payment thereof.

Rule 7(5) contemplates interest on refund based on the final assessment. [Para 18]

While levy of interest is a part of the adjective law, yet to levy interest there must be substantive provision. Demand for interest can be made only if the legislature has specifically intended collection of interest. [Para 22]

HEADNOTE: Section 4 read with section 3 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Valuation of excisable goods - CE TI/11B - Assessable value--Taxes on raw materials--Lubricating Oils

FACT: The appellants process and manufacture in Calcutta, blended and compounded lubricating oils which fall under Central Excise T.I. 11B. They received raw materials from outside Calcutta which were liable to octroi. Collection of this tax was postponed till clearance of the finished goods from the factory. The Department held that as the octroi was part of the price of the raw materials it would form a part of the assessable value of the finished goods. The appellants argued that as per the contract, the buyer was to bear the octroi charges, therefore, such charges could not be included in the sale price.

HELD: Taxes paid on raw materials are part of the price of the finished goods and as such have to be included in the assessable value. "Under section 4(4) (d) (ii) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, the appellants are entitled to ask for exclusion of the taxes paid on the finished goods, which are the subject of assessment, but not of the taxes paid on the raw materials which go into the manufacture of the finished goods..."

FACT: The assessee-company, a tax resident of UAE , was engaged in the business of operation of ships in the international traffic and had earned freight income from the same and claimed that same was exempt under article 8 of India-UAE DTAA. It also received Inland haulage charges (IHC) for transportation of containers from Inland to port for further transportation in international traffic.

The Assessing Officer held that since the assessee had Permanent Establishment (PE) in India, the benefit of article 8 of DTAA was not available to the assessee. Hence, he made an addition of 7.5 per cent of gross receipts by applying rule 10. Further, he also made an addition on account of Inland Haulage Charges (IHC) received by the assessee.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: Additions in respect of Freight Income

Undisputedly, the facts in the instant case are identical to the facts in the assessee's own case in assessment year 2016-17 namely Avana Global FZCO v. DCIT (IT) [2021] 130 taxmann.com 481/191 ITD 627 (Mum. - Trib.). The co-ordinate bench after examining the facts had held that benefit of article 8 must be extended to entire freight receipts-irrespective of whether the earnings are relating to feeder vessels or by the ships in international traffic. In the absence of any contrary material, no reason is to be seen to take a different view. Following the aforesaid order, grounds of the appeal is to be allowed. [Para 8]

Addition in respect of Inland Haulage Charges (IHC)

Article 8 of DTAA deals with profits derived by operation of ships in international traffic. Clause 2(b) of article 8 refers to profit from the rental of ship including operation of container and related equipment used in connection with operation of ships in international traffic. Though article 8 of India-UAE DTAA does not spell out explicitly that rental of containers include trailers and related equipment for the transport of container as has been mentioned in India-Belgium DTAA article 8(2)(c) or India-Denmark DTAA article 9(4)(b), nevertheless, considering the nature of activity and the services provided by the assessee to its customers vide a composite bill of lading it can be safely inferred that the activity of Inland Haulage is directly connected with transportation of goods in international traffic. The leg of transportation of containers from Inland to Port for further transportation in International traffic is a composite activity for which single bill of lading is issued by the assessee. [Para 13]

In this case, bond says nothing about any interest and hence, on this ground alone, no interest is payable - Even otherwise, there was no provision for charge of interest in case of provisional assessment, before amendment in section 18 from 13-7-2006 - Since in this case, period involved and date of order final assessment was prior to 13-7-2006, no interest could be charged [Paras 20 to 26] [In favour of assessee] Section 3(1), read with section 3A, of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and section 68 of the Finance Act, 1996 - Charge/levy - Additional Duty of Customs/CVD - Period June 1998 to August 1998 - Department sought inclusion of anti-dumping duty in 'value' for purpose of charge of additional duty of customs - Assessee argued that only any sum chargeable 'as an addition to, and in same manner as', a duty of customs, can be added and same would refer only to surcharges and not an independent levy like anti-dumping duty - HELD : Words 'as an addition to' (along with 'in same manner') are different from 'in addition to' and therefore, same would refer to 'surcharges' only and not to independent duty like anti-dumping duty - Anti-dumping duty apart from being a separate levy from a levy of customs duty is also levied in a completely different manner from that of customs duty - Further, after 2002, sections 3(2) and 3A(2) have been amended so as to expressly exclude Anti-dumping duty from 'value' - Hence, anti-dumping would not form part of 'value' for charge of additional duty of customs [Paras 32 to 36] [In favour of assessee]

Section 112, read with section 111, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Penalty - Smuggling/illegal Import - On failure to fulfil export obligation, department made demanded duties on duty-free imports along with penalty - Assessee challenged penalties - HELD : Assessee had not diverted goods meant for export to domestic tariff area - Market considerations made it difficult, if not impossible, for assessee to fulfil its export obligations - Therefore, penalty imposed ought to be set aside [Para 37] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of pig iron.

During the period June 1998 to August 1998, the assessee imported Low Ash Metallurgical (LAM) Coke under seven Bills of Entry, against four advance licenses without payment of —

basic customs duty (BCD) levied under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962,

special customs duty (SCD) levied under section 68 of the Finance Act, 1996,

special additional duty (SAD) levied under section 3A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and

anti-dumping duty (ADD) levied under section 9A of Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

The department sought to deny exemptions on failure to fulfil export obligation.

Pending final adjudication of notice by the Commissioner, the assessee duly paid the entire duty payable towards BCD, SAD and SCD after considering partial exports already made. The assessee did not make any payment towards ADD.

The department confirmed duty demands along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent as per bond.

Tribunal enhanced ADD as per revised notification but reduced interest to 15 per cent.

The assessee challenged Anti-dumping duty, interest and penalty and other computations.

Assessee's Arguments

Basic customs duty and the special customs duty as well as special additional duty was payable by the assessee.

However, anti-dumping duty was not payable at all, as assessee was exempt under Notification No. 69 of 2000.

Notification No. 30 of 1997 did not stipulate that in the event of default, interest would become payable; hence, interest was not payable.

Since assessment was provisional, there was no provision for collection of interest for the period in dispute as section 18 was amended to include such a provision only prospectively with effect from 2006.

In any case, Anti-dumping duty could not be added for purposes of computing customs duty, special customs duty and special additional duty.

Also no penalty is imposable inasmuch as nothing contumacious was done by the assessee and the export obligation could not be fulfilled only because of bona fide commercial impossibility.

Since appeal before Tribunal was filed by assessee, he could not be worse off in an appeal filed only by the assessee herein to CESTAT and that on the assumption that the assessee was liable to pay anti-dumping duty, they should only pay the said duty at the lower rate prescribed by the Commissioner as revenue had not appealed to the Tribunal against the Commissioner's order.

Revenue's Arguments

The exemption contained in Anti-dumping duty Notification 69 of 2000 was only prospective and, hence Anti-dumping duty had to be paid for the relevant period.

Interest was payable as Notification No. 30 of 1997 independently levied a charge of interest.

Order of Tribunal was correct in law.

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Demurrage charges and Despatch money - not to be added prior to 2.3.2001 - Appeals allowed (Para 4)
Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 Assessable value - Service charges - paid to canalising agency - not deductable on the ground that it casts heavy burden of duty on the appellants (Para 8)

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Rule 9 (1)(b) of Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Project management, Engineering management and studies, Conceptual detailed layout, Stress analysis subcontractor coordination  supervision and Mathematical mooring system service charges - entire value of such services cannot be added to assessable value - about 50% of value can be estimated that will be relatable to equipment imported which is to be included (Paras 45  46)

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Rule 9 (1)(b)(iv) of Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Marine work service charges -relating to LNG Jetty for which considerable support by design and engineering were provided and engineering work had to be undertaken by service contractor are liable to be included in the value (Para 44)
Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Demurrage charges - not includible (Para 6)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods of Customs - Assessable value - Additional Transportation charges - for carrying goods by barges from mother ship to Jetty - not includible when freight charges upto Jetty have been paid by importer - appeal allowed (Paras 61  64)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Landing charges - not to be added to CIF price if the same are already included in CIF price and paid by the supplier/shipper to the port trust

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods of customs - Assessable value can differ due to variation in freight etc. Deduction of freight expenses allowed to the extent of 35% instead of 25%. ITC - import invalid since it was delayed and no application was made for extension

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable Value - insurance charges - insurance amount covering customs duty not includable in CIF value as it relates to post importation factor - appeal allowed

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Despatch money allowance - for quick turn around of vessel, and Penalty allowance - given by charter/supplier for late arrival of vessel - deductible (Para 8)

Section 14, read with  section 151A, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Levy of, and exemption from, customs duties - Valuation of goods for purposes of assessment - Whether when circular issued by Central Board of Excise and Customs (Board) remains in operation, revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to terms of statute - Held, yes - Whether circular issued by Board in which it was said that demurrage did not form part of assessable value of goods imported, same was binding on revenue and department could not contend otherwise - Held, yes

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Valuation; Assessable value has to include unloading charges also, not merely port charges: but any bonus earned for quick unloading should be deducted

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 and Rule 9 of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Assessable value - Stevedoring charges - for bagging and stitching - includible - appeal rejected (Paras 13  14)

Section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Assessable value - Interest - for delayed payment - not charged over and above invoice price which is same in all cases - deduction of such interest not admissible - appeal dismissed (Para 3)

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - High sea sales - Rule 9(1)(e) of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Demurrage, Wharfage and Stock loss charges - goods purchased by respondents on high sea sales on payment of amount inclusive of such charges in terms of high sea sale agreement and final invoices raised on them - includible - appeals allowed. [Majority order]. (Paras 8,15  18)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Stevedoring charges - expenses incurred for unloading the goods from the ship - not to be added where landing charges as percentage of value of the goods are added to arrive at the assessable value - appeal allowed (Para 9)
Assessable value - Section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Interest - on delayed payments - not includible - appeal allowed (Para 4)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for custom - Reference to Larger Bench - Assessable value - Demurrage charges - whether demurrage charges could be excluded from assessable value in cases of imports made after 2.3.2001 even where assessments were provisional - referred to Larger Bench in view of doubts about correctness of CESTAT's earlier judgments (Paras 8  9)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Rule 9(c) of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Valuation of goods for customs - Assessable value - Capital goods - charges paid towards post importation activities such as erection, commissioning and training - not to be added - appeal allowed (Para 7)
Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Stevedoring charges - not to be added as already included in landing charges @ 0.9% added to the value (Para 2)
Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Landing charges - on notional basis and not actual charges incurred, to be added to arrive at the assessable value - appeal dismissed (Para 5)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Lighterage charges - Transportation charges from anchorage to port jetty by barges - transaction value is CIF - said charges not includible - appeal allowed (Paras 6  7)

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962- Rule 9 (2) of Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Freight - goods came to Chennai/Vishakhapatnam by mother vessel and transshipped to Haldia/Budge Budge by daughter vessel because of draft restrictions - actual cost of transportation by daughter vessel to be added as it is not included in FOB or CF invoice price and is paid separately (Paras 6.2  7)
Section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Assessable value - Interest on delayed payment - not to be added to value (Paras 6  11)
Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Transportation cost - price payable on a Time Charter cannot be treated as cost of trans-portation - not includible (Paras 3  5)

Assessable value — Rule 9 of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Machinery - charges for conducting test on raw materials and finished goods - not addable being post commencement of production charges (Para 7)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Valuation of goods for customs - Freight - Demurrage charges - paid for rentention of vessel beyond free lay time - not to be added for period prior to 26.9.2006 - appeals allowed (Para 10.1)

Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Assessable value - Interpretative Notes - Charges or Costs - not covered by clauses (a) to (c) - not available for inclusion in value of imported goods.

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962-Rule 9 (2)of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Assessable value - Freight and Insurance charges -goods imported by air - invoice shows freight and insurance charges separately - 20% of FOB value as per invoice in terms of Rule 9 (2) and not actual freight and insurances charges, should have been added to FOB price in invoice - appeal allowed (Para 3)
Section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Assessable value - Interest - on delayed payment - not to be added. (Para 3)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Assessable value - Bagging charges - goods imported in bulk - bagged after unloading from ship - since importation is complete when goods landed on landmass, bagging charges are not includible - Revenue's appeal dismissed (Para 3)

"The aforesaid provisions of the Act, therefore, clearly show that after the imported goods are discharged from the vessel at the wharf the importer cannot immediately take delivery thereof. The imported goods remain in the custody of the Port Trust Authorities till they are, inter alia, cleared for home consumption. This being the position the goods cannot be cleared and delivery taken without their being valued and assessed and, thereafter, duty being paid. Section 14 of the Act provides that the value of the goods shall be deemed to be the price of the goods for the delivery at the time and place of importation in the course of international trade. The value has to be determined with relation to the time when physical delivery to the importer can take place. Physical delivery can take place only after the bill of entry, inter alia, for home consumption is filed and it is the value at that point of time which would be relevant. It is evident that there normally will be some lapse of time between the time when the shipper discharges the goods and the time when the bill of entry is filed. The landing charges, which are imposed at or after the time of the discharge of the goods and prior to the clearance being granted under Section 47 of the Act, necessarily have to be an element which have to be taken into account in determining the value thereof for the purpose of assessing the customs duty which would be chargeable" (Para 14)

Valuation -  (Customs) - All service transactions relating to imported goods was not includible in assessable value of goods - Service rendered in India after import, even if directly related to imported goods, could not justifiably enhance assessable value - Inclusion of 'cost of services' was to be ascertained as per Rule 10 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 [Rule 10 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007] [Para 14]

Assessable value - Section 4 (1) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Interest on receivables - charged on delayed payments after interest free period of 15 days - deductible even when not shown separately on invoice - appeal allowed (Para 8)

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Transportation charges - Use of word 'to' and 'at' as prefixes to phrase 'place of importation' in Rules 9(2)(a) and 9(2)(b) ibid brings out distinction between transport charges and unloading/handling charges and latter does not include barge charges being transport charges - Includible in value - Appeal dismissed (Paras 10  14)
Section 14 of Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Assessable value - Coal - Demurrage charges - not includable in assessable value - Revenue's appeal dismissed. (Para 5)

The respondent imported various petroleum products and crude oil into India and had cleared the same upon payment of customs duty. The customs authorities having noted that the respondent had paid demurrage charges to the shipowners under the charter party agreements through negotiating bank issued a show-cause notice to the appellant and included the bank charges and demurrage paid in the customs value of the goods and created additional demand of customs duty against the respondent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order. On second appeal, the Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal (CEGAT) allowed the appeal of the respondent on the grounds; (i) that the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) had issued a circular on 14-8-1991 under section 151A of the Customs Act in which it was said that the demurrage did not form part of the assessable value of the goods imported and the circular was binding on the revenue and the department could not contend otherwise, (ii) that the decision of the Supreme Court in Garden Silk Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [1999] 113 ELT 358 relied upon by the revenue was not an authority for the proposition that demurrage payable on account of delay in discharging goods from a vessel was includible in the value of goods while assessing the customs duty payable thereon, and (iii) that under section 14 the assessable value of the imported goods must be the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold and the payment of demurrage was not an incident of an ordinary sale and an extraordinary expenditure, like demurrage, could not be included in the assessable value of the imported goods.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The question involved in the instant appeal is as to whether ship demurrage charges paid by the assessee-importer on the import of the goods were to be included in the assessable value of the goods imported for purpose of levy of customs duty.

The point for decision in the appeal is whether rule 9 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 prescribes the inclusion of demurrage charges in the assessable value. The appellants have sought waiver of pre-deposit of Customs duty demanded from them on the demurrage charges incurred by them.

All these 153 appeals raise a common set of points, viz., (1) whether notional landing charges are includible for computing the assessable value of imported goods; (2) whether customs and auxiliary duties are includible in the aggregate value of the goods for purpose of levy of addl. duty (CVD) of customs, and (3) whether packing charges are excludible from the assessable value in terms of Notfn. 184/76-Cus.

The appellants process and manufacture in Calcutta, blended and compounded lubricating oils which fall under Central Excise T.I. 11B. They received raw materials from outside Calcutta which were liable to octroi. Collection of this tax was postponed till clearance of the finished goods from the factory. The Department held that as the octroi was part of the price of the raw materials it would form a part of the assessable value of the finished goods. The appellants argued that as per the contract, the buyer was to bear the octroi charges, therefore, such charges could not be included in the sale price.
The issue under dispute was whether overtime charges paid to customs officers should be included in the assessable value of fertilizers imported by the appellant.

The assessees challenged constitutional validity of proviso (ii) of rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 inserted by Notification No. 39/90, dated 5-7-1990.

The assessee claimed that the actual loading, unloading and handling charges amounted to Rs. 69.98 paisa as per the tariff of the International Airport Authority of India, Madras (now Chennai). However, the Customs Authorities, on the basis of the impugned notification added a sum of Rs. 15,214.69 paisa at 1 per cent of CIF value.

The assessee argued that such a notional fixation of the handling charges with the addition of 1 per cent of CIF value, irrespective of the nature of goods, size of the cargo, was in total disregard to total handling charges, even when such actual handling charges could be ascertained. Same was irrational, arbitrary and ultra vires.

The department argued that it was found impossible to ascertain the actual amounts incurred towards loading, unloading and handling charges while making the assessment as they varied depending upon the quantities and place of import. Finding this difficulty in actual practice and in order to achieve certainty, one per cent of the CIF value was fixed to be included in the assessable value. It was argued that once this uniformity is achieved with the aforesaid provisions, merely because some would be getting the benefit while others would suffer certain detriment, is no reason for invalidating the provision when many others would be getting the benefit thereof as well. The percentage had been fixed by the rule making authority after taken into consideration the overall picture.

The appellants in all these cases imported small consignments through shipping lines. These goods were landed and delivered by the shipping company without any extra charge as freight, including landing charges, was paid by the shipping company. The Collector (Appeals) contended that import of goods is not complete till they are landed, pass through Port Trust and are placed before Customs for assessment, and that landing charges should be included in the assessable value. He also added that there is no documentary evidence or receipt to show that the freight paid included landing charges.

On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the Constitution of India does not empower the Parliament to provide for the mode of determining assessable value by loading c.i.f. value with customs duty for the purpose of payment of CVD under the Customs Tariff Act. It was also contended that the Parliament though entitled to provide for double taxation was not entitled to levy taxes by adding the basic customs duty to c.i.f. value as that amounted to tax on tax.

Facts

Assessee imported crude oil, which was liable to duty on ad valorem basis.

Department demanded duty on quantity of crude oil mentioned in bills of lading.

Assessee argued that since quantity actually received into shore tanks in India was lesser, quantity actually received should be basis for payment of duty.

Revenue's Arguments

The department argued that since duty was now levied on an ad valorem basis and not on a specific rate, the duty should be paid on the bill of lading quantity based on the ullage obtained when the goods were loaded on the vessel in the country of export.

Since full payment for the goods has to be made by the importer only on the basis of the quantity mentioned in the bill of lading, therefore the 'transaction value' of the said goods would only be as per the payment made of the amounts stated in the bill of lading and not the quantity received ultimately in the shore tanks at ports in India.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee argued that it makes no difference as to whether the basis for customs duty is at a specific rate or is ad valorem, quantity of goods at the time of import alone is to be looked at.

Taxable event is only when goods are imported, and that therefore valuation at the time of import alone has to be looked at.

The appellants manufacture acetylene gas which they deliver in cylinders supplied by the customers. The cost of maintenance, handling and the statutory testing of cylinders is recovered from the customers, and the appellants sought exemption of these charges from the assessable value on the ground that they were a part of the cost of the cylinder, which is non-dutiable. The Dept. held that all such charges incurred within the factory were includible in the assessable value and disallowed the abatement.

Delivery and collection charges for oxygen gas supplied to buyers was the issue under dispute. The excise authorities contended that the charges should be included in the assessable value while the respondents stated that the prices were ex-factory, exclusive of post manufacturing expenses and did not have any bearing on manufacturing costs. They further contended that the cylinders in which the gas was delivered were durable and returnable containers and, therefore, could not be included in the assessable value. It was also pointed out that the show cause notices were time-barred under Rule 10.

The appellants manufacture aerated waters and sell their products to various wholesale dealers from whom they recover an additional Rs. 5/- per crate as hire charges on account of delay in return of empties and Rs. 3/- per crate as compensation for not lifting the agreed quantity. Having intercepted a truck belonging to another company, carrying aerated water bottles, issued by the appellants the Collector confiscated the goods, denied the benefit of Notfn. 175/86-CE on the ground that the appellants' clearances were to be clubbed with those of the other company and raised a demand of Rs. 4,02,754/- holding that the compensation amount of Rs. 3/- per crate, a proportionate part of the Rs. 5/- levied as container hire and 80 paise per crate towards transportation charges are includible in the assessable value. He also imposed a penalty.

The questions for consideration before the High Court were as to whether the amount representing sale value of nominations obtained against import entitlements was assessable as business income and whether the amount representing transportation charges of goods incurred within India upto the port would rank for deduction under section 35B

The applicant is into the business of supplying edible oil and imports edible grade crude oil without any separate charges for transportation from other countries to the Indian port on CIF basis. When it enters the Indian port, basic customs duty and applicable cess along with IGST is paid.

In the instant application, the applicant has sought advance ruling in respect of the question as to whether under Reverse Charge Mechanism, IGST should be paid by the importer on ocean freight in the case of CIF basis contract.

The applicant-company 'E' is engaged in the business of manufacturing and supplying Transformer components.

The applicant 'E' is importing goods from the holding company located at Turkey for which the payment terms is 120 days from the date of invoice for import of goods and if the company 'E' located at India does not pay to holding company located at Turkey (outside India) on due date, the holding company is charging interest on late payment; that the company has obtained bank credit facility from CITI Bank based on the Corporate Guarantee issued by holding company and they have paid Stamp tax in Turkey as per their land rules and they have raised reimbursement invoice of said payment to 'E' India; that the company is importing goods on CIF basis (cost including freight) and the invoice that is raised by the seller is clearly showing the amount of Sea freight and it is also noted that at the time of Bill of Entry, the assessable value calculated for payment of IGST includes the value of Sea Freight, hence, IGST is already paid on the value of sea freight at the time of customs clearance.

The applicant is seeking Advance Ruling on the question as to whether liability to pay GST on Reverse charge arises if amount is paid as interest on late payment of invoices of imported goods and whether liability to pay GST on Reverse charge arises if amount is paid for reimbursement of Stamp tax paid as a pure agent by 'E' Turkey on applicant's behalf.

The appellants had imported two Toyota Corona 1600 DLX Sedans. They presented the manufacturer's invoice at the lime of assessment of Customs duly. The Customs authorities determined duty payable after adding freight, insurance and landing charges to the invoice price. Though the importers claimed 15% discount on the manufacturer's price, as well as exclusion of freight, insurance and landing charges, these claims were rejected by the Asstt. Collr. On appeal the Tribunal upheld the Asstt. Collr.'s valuation. Depreciation claims in respect of car accessories like stereo AC were also disallowed. After this the importers submitted applications for rectification of mistakes which, they argued, were obvious and apparent in the earlier order. Their main contention is that as value should have been fixed at place of removal (the market in Japan) insurance and transportation expenses etc., were to be deducted. Besides, the Department was bound by promissory estoppel to allow a discount of 15% in view of a Departmental circular providing for this discount.

The applicant is engaged in the trading of various edible oils which fall under chapter 15 of GST Tariff. The Applicant intends to import crude soyabean oil on CIF basis which includes the component of Ocean Freight in the price of imported goods.

The applicant is required to authorize the seller who is a person located in non-taxable Territory for transporting the above goods by a vessel from supplier's place in Indian Custom station. The seller collects the ocean freight in the price of goods from the buyer i.e. the applicant.

As per corrigendum issued on 30-6-2017 to the Notification No. 8/2017-IT (R), the importer of the goods is required to pay IGST on Reverse charge Mechanism on the amount of deemed ocean freight equal to 10 per cent of the value of goods imported.

The Applicant, has posed question and seeking rule as to whether the applicant/importer is again required to pay IGST on the component of ocean freight under RCM on deemed amount to double taxation of IGST on deemed components of Ocean Freight of the imported goods.

The assessee was engaged in manufacturing and trading of products like de-oiled meals, industrial hard oils, edible oils, marine products, emergency lighting units and soaps, etc.

It entered into an import agreement with importers in terms of which the imported material was to be purchased by the assessee at landed cost i.e. CIF price, custom duty, clearing charges, etc.

At the time of actual import of material by the importers, the Custom Department demanded 100 per cent of the applicable custom duty as additional customs duty on the CIF value of imported material.

Against said demand, importers filed a writ petition wherein the Supreme Court allowed the clearance of imported material on payment of 15% of the disputed additional custom duty and granted stay for balance 85% of the said duty, pending the final decision in the writ petition.

The stay granted by the Supreme Court was subject to furnishing of bank guarantees by the importers in favour of the department for the unpaid amount of disputed duty.

As per import agreement, the assessee provided counter guarantees for the bank guarantees provided by the importers for the unpaid disputed amount of customs duty i.e. 85% of the additional customs duty.

In return of income, the assessee claimed deduction on account of the said additional custom duty, in-as-much as the same was included in the landed cost of imported material.

The Assessing Officer rejected assessee's claim holding that liability of payment of additional custom duty had not been crystallised during relevant assessment year.

The Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing and selling of two-wheelers in joint venture with a Japanese company. During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer referred the case to the Transfer Pricing Officer, as there were certain international transaction with its associated enterprises (AEs). It purchased material on CIF basis and ordinarily included freight and cost of delivery of goods in purchase price. However, in exceptional circumstances, where assessee has to immediately lift material, transport charges were not included in purchase price, but were separately debited to profit and loss account, since invoices of transporters were received after consumption of material.

The Assessing Officer added the amount of freight inward and import clearing expenses to cost of closing inventory. The assessee contended that the revenue had accepted its method of valuation in the past. It also contended that the transaction would be revenue neutral in the long run, as similar adjustment would also be required in the opening stock. However, the Dispute Resolution Panel confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On assessee's appeal:

The revenue authorities, while assessing the value of superfine cement manufactured by the appellants, added packing charges to the price on the ground that the assessable value should be inclusive of packing charges. The appellants contended that superfine cement was not different from ordinary grey portland cement for which packing charges were not included in the assessable value and therefore should also be excluded for their goods. They sought adjournment of the case till the Supreme Court clarified the issue of 'durable and returnable packing'.

The assessee claimed that the wharfage charge, which is a statutory port due was eligible for deductions from value of custom house agent services for calculating its taxable value. In the impugned order, the Commissioner (Appeals) had not granted the benefit of deduction on the ground that as per the Board’s Circular F. No. B/43/1/97-TRU, dated 6-6-1997, the assessee was allowed to treat 15 per cent lump-sum receipts as value of taxable services and pay service tax on this 15 per cent only. According to him if said deduction was allowed, the residual payment could not be treated as lump-sum payment and service tax liability would have to be discharged on total receipts minus deductions and not on 15 per cent of total receipts minus deductions. On the issue of time bar, he had noted that the assessee was regularly furnishing returns, which were assessed and finalized by the Department and, therefore, the larger period could not be invoked. However, for another part of the period, he had noted that once self-assessment procedure was adopted, the liability of calculating and discharging duty was of the assessee alone and no knowledge on the part of the Department could be presumed and for that period, the charge of concealment resulting in short payment of duty became sustainable.

On appeal :

The matter is an application for stay of the order of the Collector (Appeals) setting aside the order of the lower authority for loading the assessable value of the imported goods with (i) the value of instructions documents, drawings and design materials, and (ii) interest on advances made.

The assessee a trading concern exported molasses worth Rs.6,14,87,164. As per the terms and conditions of the sale, demurrage and dead freight incurred by virtue of delay in loading molasses at Port had to be borne by the foreign buyer and the same was to be paid to the Chartered Ship owners. Foreign buyer in turn, collected the demurrage and dead freight charges from the assessee on the ground that the delay in loading was attributable to the assessee. Thus, instead of the assessee paying the amount towards demurrage and dead freight, the purchaser, a foreign buyer deducted the said amount from the sale consideration and remitted the balance sale proceeds to the assessee company. The assessee submitted that the deduction under section 80HHC has to be worked out on the sale consideration of Rs.6,14,87,164.

The Assessing Officer rejected the said claim and restricted the deduction only to the net amount received by the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On further appeal, the Tribunal, pointed out that the issue had to be seen in the context of the agreement between the assessee and the foreign company. Consequently, it remitted the matter back to the Assessing Officer to give a finding from the materials on record as to whether this sum were actually of such nature to be borne by the assessee.

On instant appeal by revenue to the High Court:
The petitioner claimed that transport charges received by the petitioner from the Indian Oil Corporation were not liable to be assessed.

The appellants manufactured metal containers from the steel sheets/coils supplied to them by Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (HPCL) under an agreement on recovery of fabrication charges. The assessable value of the containers was determined on the basis of declared cost of steel sheets and fabrication charges. The Department sought to add customers' notional profit margin of 10% to the assessable value. This was proposed to be added on the ground that the goods were fabricated on behalf of HPCL and therefore the notional profit becomes an element of cost so far as HPCL is concerned. Transportation charges incurred on steel sheets from the railway siding to the factory and cost of wrapping material received was also proposed to be added to the assessable value.

The Assessing Officer found during the assessment proceedings that in the books of account of the assessee, huge liabilities on account of brokerage, forwarding agency commission (FAC) and terminal handling charges (THC) due to the principals were reflected. When confronted, the assessee while furnishing detailed break-up of those liabilities, explained that the entire freight collections were deposited in the bank accounts of its principals in India, however, the receipts on account of THC and detention charges as also brokerage and FAC were deposited separately in its own bank account, as per the RBI guidelines. It further claimed that those accounts were operated by it only on behalf of its principals and the amounts deposited therein were used only for meeting various expenditure on account of brokerage, FAC, THC and detention charges, which were payable on behalf of its principals. The Assessing Officer, however, observing, inter alia, that the assessee was benefited since without paying any taxes it was able to have control over a big chunk of funds, which it was not required to pay to anyone, i.e., neither to the creditors since they did not exist nor to the principals since the amount was non-repatriable, treated the same as bogus liabilities and added the same to its income accordingly. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), while finding that the assessee had actually remitted detention charges of Rs. 2,14,78,504 to its principals as cleared by the RBI, subsequent to the block period, confirmed the impugned additions except with regard to the said detention charges to the extent such charges were actually remitted subsequently to the principals.

On cross appeal :

Facts

A dispute arose as to whether the cheque discounting charges are includible in the assessable value or not.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that cheque discounting charges are includible in the assessable value.

The assessee argued that Cheque discounting charges are just like interest on receivable, which are not includible in the assessable value.

Issue Involved

Whether cheque discounting charges are includible in value ?

Facts

The assessee was manufacturer of Paper and Paper Board chargeable to Central Excise duty.

The assessee recovered —

dharmada charges @ 0.25% of the value of the goods from their customers ;

Department sought to include these charges in value of goods.

Assessee's Arguments

Transit insurance charges and freight charges were not includible in value —

in respect of the period prior to 01/07/2000, there was a specific provision sub-section (2) for section 4 providing for exclusion of the freight charges from the assessable value,

in respect of the period with effect from 01/7/2000, in accordance with the provisions of Rule 5 of the Central Excise Valuation Rules, 2000, the charges for freight and transit insurance were not includible in the assessable value when the same are separately shown in the invoices.

Though in this case, the freight and transit insurance were not mentioned in the Central Excise invoices, the same had been charged separately by debit notes and this amounts to charging separately for the freight and transit insurance.

In any case, since the sale of the goods was from the factory gate, the freight and insurance charges cannot be included in the assessable value.

The dharmada charges are also not includible in the assessable value.

Revenue's Arguments

With regard to freight and transit insurance, since the same have not been shown separately in the invoices, in view of Rule 5 of the Central Excise Valuation Rules, the same have to be included in the assessable value.

As regards dharmada charges, in view of judgment of the Apex Court in the case of CCE v. Panchmukhi Engg. Works 2003 (158) E.L.T. 550 (S.C.), the same were includible in value.

Whether the charges, as aforesaid, were includible in value ?
