A cursory reading of section 14 makes it clear that customs duty is chargeable on goods by reference to their value at a price at which such goods or like goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale at the time and place of importation in the course of international trade. This would mean that any amount that is referable to the imported goods post-importation has necessarily to be excluded. It is with this basic principle in mind that the rules made under sub-clause 1(A) have been framed and have to be interpreted. [Para 7]

Under the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules of 1988, rule 2(f) defines 'transaction value' as the value determined in accordance with rule 4 of these rules. Rule 4(1) in turn states that the transaction value of imported goods shall be the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India, adjusted in accordance with the provisions of rule 9 of these rules. A reading of rule 4 and rule 9 makes it clear that only those costs and services that are actually paid or payable for imported goods pre-import are to be added for the purpose of determining the value of the imported goods. [Para 8]

On an analysis of the technical services agreement, it is clear that the assessee has only associated Met Chem Canada Inc. as a technical consultant. There is no transfer of know-how or patents, trademarks or copyright. What is clear is that technical services to be provided by Met Chem Canada Inc. is basically to co-ordinate and advise the assessee so that the assessee can successfully set up, commission and operate the plant in India. It will be noticed that co-ordination and advice is to take place post-importation in order that the plant be set up and commissioned in India. In fact, all the clauses of this agreement make it clear that such services are only post-importation. Clause 9 on which a large part of the agreements ranged again makes it clear that ownership of patents, know-how, copyright and other intellectual property rights shall remain vested in the technical consultant and none of these will be transferred to the assessee. The assessee becomes owner of that portion of documents, drawings, plans and specifications originally created by technical consultant pursuant to the agreement. This again refers only to documents, drawings etc. of setting up, commissioning and operating the plant, all of which are post-importation of the plant into India. [Para 9]

In fact, clause 13 of the purchase order is important in that liquidated damages are only payable for delay in commissioning the plant and for failure to achieve the stipulated performance, both of which are post-importation activities. [Para 10]

Another thing to be noticed is that a conjoint reading of the technical services agreement and the purchase order do not lead to the conclusion that the technical services agreement is in any way a pre-condition for the sale of the plant itself. On the contrary, as has been pointed out above, the technical services agreement read as a whole is really only to successfully set up, commission and operate the plant after it has been imported into India. It is clear, therefore, that clause 9(1)(e) would not be attracted on the facts of this case and consequently the consideration for the technical services to be provided by Met Chem Canada Inc. cannot be added to the value of the equipment imported to set up the plant in India. [Para 11]

It is clear that the facts of the present case do not attract rule 9(1)(e). Therefore, demand was set aside. [Para 18]

FACT: The appellants had imported two Toyota Corona 1600 DLX Sedans. They presented the manufacturer's invoice at the lime of assessment of Customs duly. The Customs authorities determined duty payable after adding freight, insurance and landing charges to the invoice price. Though the importers claimed 15% discount on the manufacturer's price, as well as exclusion of freight, insurance and landing charges, these claims were rejected by the Asstt. Collr. On appeal the Tribunal upheld the Asstt. Collr.'s valuation. Depreciation claims in respect of car accessories like stereo AC were also disallowed. After this the importers submitted applications for rectification of mistakes which, they argued, were obvious and apparent in the earlier order. Their main contention is that as value should have been fixed at place of removal (the market in Japan) insurance and transportation expenses etc., were to be deducted. Besides, the Department was bound by promissory estoppel to allow a discount of 15% in view of a Departmental circular providing for this discount.

HELD: Rectification application cannot be used for re-arguing those points which were already discussed and settled by the Tribunal. As there is no apparent misapplication of law by the Tribunal, earlier decision cannot be disturbed. "under the garb of a rectification application, it is not open to a party to avail it as a further chance of re-arguing the matter or calling upon the Tribunal to review the basis of the decision. Such a course would be beyond the scope of an application for rectification. The "mistakes" repeatedly urged by the applicants were the contentions raised in the main appeals and Tribunal has taken a particular view. It may be argued that they are debatable conclusions. But rectification applications are not intended for re-opening a decision."

Valuation: Tribunal decision that valuation is to be based on prices at the point of landing is upheld. Hence adding of freight, insurance etc. are correct. Deduction of 15% from market price on ground of promissory estoppel is not relevant because the calculation was based on the manufacturer's invoice, whereas deductions were allowed in those cases where the calculation was based on international prices (in. the absence of manufacturer's invoice). "The Tribunal has in the main order held that the prices at which the goods were delivered at the point of landing in India was relevant and not the price at which the transactions took place in Tokyo. The adding of freight, insurance and landing charges was held to be correct. The claim for discount was rejected by the Tribunal for the reasons already stated. The Assessment of the air-conditioners and other accessories were upheld on merits. As rightly urged by the JDR, no promissory estoppel would arise."

Due to long durational process involved in the investigation of the related party transaction, SVB investigations in the following cases should not be initiated looking at the revenue implications -

Locations and Jurisdiction of SVB Units:

The Special Valuation Branches are currently functional at following Customs location houses i.e., Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi, Mumbai. Further, the jurisdiction of SVB would entirely be dependent on the corporate or registered office of the importer, whichever is nearby and convenient to the importer.

The importer is given free hand to choose which SVB he wants to approach for the cases which require investigation by the SVB. Once a particular import transaction has triggered investigation at one SVB, then the same needs to be communicated by the customs houses to other SVBs as well for the better compliance of the process involved.

Procedure for investigation under SVB :

Finalization of Assessment :

Upon receipt of Investigation report from the Special Valuation branch, there could be two scenarios which could affect the assessment -

a.

Declared Value is found confirming to Rule 3: Where the declared value as per Bill of Entry has been found confirming to the relevant rule of the CVR,2007 - the provisional assessment done by the customs houses shall be considered the final assessment and accordingly it must be finalized.

b.

Declared Value is found not confirming to Rule 3: Where the declared value as per Bill of Entry is found to be influenced by the relationship or such case as may be applicable, the proper office of the customs house shall issue a show cause notice to the importer within 15 days of the receipt of the Investigation Report (IR) from the Special Valuation Branch (SVB).

Wherever the imports have been cleared through multiple locations, jurisdictional commissioner shall after consulting with other locations, make a proposal for appointment of common adjudicating authority for the matter and after providing enough opportunity to the importer, pass a combined order quantifying the extent of influence on the declared transaction value.

Concept of Extra Duty Deposit/Revenue Deposit :

As per Circular No. 01/98 dated 1-1-1988, there was a duty called extra duty deposit which was applicable in cases where the documents sought for are not provided to the relevant authorities failing for which the higher extra duty deposit shall be leviable. However, in the circular issued in 2016, board has reviewed the levy and has clarified that no security in form of extra duty deposit shall be obtained from the importers, but if the importer fails to provide the information within 60 days of such requisition, security deposit at a higher rate of 5% shall be imposed by the commissioner which shall be valid for the period of 3 months.

[Same principle should apply to sales and distribution expenses incurred by brand name/copyright owner].

Advertisement expenses incurred by assessee himself - Advertisement expenses incurred by assessee himself are obviously includible - DCM Engineering Products v. CCE (2011) 268 ELT 396 (CESTAT) [Issue so obvious that it is not clear why assessee went in appeal at all. In fact, normally, such expenses are included in the selling price itself].

Training charges to customer

12.8-1 Training charges to customer will be includible if they are in connection with sale or by reason of sale. If the transaction of providing training to employees of customer is an independent transaction, it may be 'in relation to sale', but not 'in connection with sale'.

Training charges are not includible in assessable value - CCE v. Real Time Systems (2009) 237 ELT 289 (CESTAT).

Training or training aids for use of missiles is post-sales activity and is not includible in assessable value - Brahmos Aerospace P Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 795 (CESTAT).

In Decibells Electronics P Ltd. v. CCE - 1996 (88) ELT 181 (CEGAT), it was held that consultancy charges for training of customer's staff in relation to the product are not includible. - followed in Gallium Equipment P Ltd. v. CCE 1998(98) ELT 96 (CEGAT) - same view in National Radio v. CCE 1999(105) ELT 59 (CEGAT) * Computer Peripheral Devices v. CCE 1999(105) ELT 510 (CEGAT) * Minicomp v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 34 (CEGAT).

Liquidated damages for late delivery or breach of contract payable/receivable

12.8-2 Liquidated damages may be either payable or receivable by assessee.

Liquidated damages payable - Some contracts make provision for liquidated damages where an amount is deducted if delivery is not effected in time or some other condition of contract is violated. 'Transaction Value' means the price actually paid or payable for goods. It includes any amount payable by buyer at the time of the sale or at any other time. Thus since the amount of 'liquidated damages' is not 'payable' by buyer to assessee at all, it can be argued that 'transaction value' should be calculated only after deducting the liquidated damages, i.e. it should be allowed as deduction. Counter argument can be that 'full amount' is 'payable' though actual amount paid is less on account of deduction by way of penalty. Thus, effectively, full amount is 'paid' and deduction has nothing to do with value of goods.

In United Telecom Ltd. v. CCE (2006) 204 ELT 626 (CESTAT), price was reduced by customer for late delivery of goods. It was held that such compensation paid to buyer is liquidated damages and not in nature of penalty. It will be allowable as deduction and duty paid in excess is refundable. It was held that ratio of decisions under old section 4 cannot be made applicable to new section 4 which has come into effect from 1-7-2000 - followed in CCE v. HFCL (2008) 231 ELT 307 (CESTAT).

This view has been confirmed in CCE v. Victory Electricals Ltd. (2014) 43 GST 649 = 42 taxmann.com 215 = 298 ELT 534 (CESTAT LB), where it was held that after such liquidated damages (even if termed as penalty), the transaction value is reduced. Excise duty is payable on such lower value only - followed in CCE v. HFCL (Wireless Division) (2014) 46 GST 664 = 47 taxmann.com 171 (CESTAT).

However, the importer can hardly be heard to say that its invoice value did not represent the correct value of imported goods - Punjab Processors v. CC 2003 (157) ELT 625 (SC).

6.2-6 Duel price in case of service parts and OE

It is standard universal practice to charge lower price when the component is supplied as OE (i.e. Original Equipment) part for manufacture of machine/equipment/vehicle to a co-manufacturer and charge higher price when same component is supplied as service part i.e. spare part. [The difference can be as high as two to five times].

CBI&C has confirmed, vide its circular No. MFCA(DR) No. 82-2002-Cus.V dated 3-12-2002, that such duel pricing is acceptable and both can be treated as 'transaction value' if other requirements of section 14 are fulfilled. Thus, price of OE component should be inclusive of factory cost, factory overheads, administration and commercial overheads and reasonable profit margin of original manufacturer. However, related party transactions should be closely looked into and aspect of 'transfer pricing' and 'tie-in sales' should be seen.

6.2-7 Related person under Customs Valuations Provisions

Rule 2(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and Rule 2(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 define that persons shall be deemed to be 'related' only if one of the conditions is satisfied [same definition and same rule number prior to 10-10-2007]:

they are officers or directors of one other's businesses [rule 2(2)(i)]

they are legally recognised partners in business [rule 2(2)(ii)]

they are employer and employee [rule 2(2)(iii)]

Any person directly or indirectly owns, controls or holds 5% or more of shares of both of them [rule 2(2)(iv)]

one of them controls other directly or indirectly [rule 2(2)(v)]

both of them are controlled - directly or indirectly - by third person [rule 2(2)(vi)]

together they control a third person - directly or indirectly [rule 2(2)(vii)]

they are members of same family [rule 2(2)(viii)]. (what is "family" is not defined).

Person includes legal person i.e. Company, partnership firm, trust etc. [Explanation I to Rule 2(2)].

If a person is sole agent or sole distributor or sole concessionaire of other, he will be deemed to be 'related', if he falls within the criteria of rule 2(2) [Explanation II to Rule 2(2)]. Thus, sole selling agent or sole distributor or sole concessionaire will be 'related person' only if he falls within the criteria as specified in rule 2(2). A sole selling agent or sole distributor or sole concessionaire is not automatically deemed as 'related person' in all the cases.

Interpretative Note to rule 2 clarify that for purpose of rule 2(2)(v), one person is deemed to control other if he is legally or operationally in a position to exercise restraint or direction over the other. Thus, control need not be only legal - even operational control is enough.

HEADNOTE: Section  43B  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business disallowance  -  Certain deductions to be allowed only on actual payment  (Customs duty) - Assessment year  2018-19  - During year, assessee-company paid certain customs duty under protest and claimed deduction for same under section 43B - Assessing Officer disallowed same - It was noted that assessee's liability to pay customs duty arose on raising of demand by customs authorities in financial year 2017-18 when assessee imported goods for purpose of selling to its customers in India - Whether since assessee paid customs duty under protest in relevant assessment year and offered to tax amount refunded in pursuance thereof in assessment year 2020-21, impugned addition would lead to double taxation and same was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was engaged in business of marketing, distribution and after sales services of the products manufactured by Keysight Group entities under the Electronic Measurement Group business.

■

During the year under consideration, the assessee paid certain customs duty and while computing the total income, the assessee claimed a deduction under section 43B on account of payment of custom duty.

■

The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

Appellant's liability arises for payment of customs duty on raising of demand by customs authorities in FY 2017-18 as during the year appellant has imported goods for the purpose of selling to its customers in India and as per instructions of CBEC where items are imported from related party the declared import price of said items are required to be certified by Special Valuation Branch (SVB). These instructions mandate that an additional customs charge in the form of Extra Duty Depoists (EDD) of 1% is payable on provisional basis until the investigation is underway. The Appellant has paid 'Extra Duty Deposits (EDD)' in accordance with Circular No. 5/2016 issued by Central Board of Excise and Customs dated 9th February 2016. It comes up that the Appellant has in fact received a favorable order from the SVB wherein the declared price has been accepted and the refunds of the taxes paid was accordingly payable to the Appellant.[Para 5]

■

.It is settled law that once the demand has been quantified, the amount paid towards discharging the liability irrespective of the matter is pending for adjudication at higher level same is an allowable deduction. [Para 6]

■

Once the customs authority order for clearance of goods, then statutory liability of customs duty, is deemed to have incurred by the assessee in such year in which the liability has been paid. Thus, on the basis of the aforesaid discussion, section 43B permits certain deductions only on actual payment of the amounts and same provides a clear departure from the method of accounting followed by an assessee. It allows deduction of statutory liabilities in the year of payment notwithstanding the fact that the liability in respect thereof may have been incurred in another year. More so when assessee has offered to tax in assessment year 2020-21, the amount refunded in pursuance thereof and thus if the impugned addition is sustained it will lead to double taxation. In the light of the aforesaid, the grounds in both the years deserve to be sustained. The appeals of the assessee are allowed. [Para 7]

6.5

Deductive Value for customs valuation

Rule 7 [same rule number prior to 10-10-2007] of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 provide for the next i.e. fourth alternative method, which is called 'deductive method'.

If the importer requests and the Customs Officer approves, 'computed value' method as given in rule 8 can be used before the method of 'deductive value' [proviso to Rule 6 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007]

This method should be applied if transaction value of identical goods or similar goods is not available; but these products are sold in India. The assumption made in this method is that identical or similar imported goods are sold in India and its selling price in India is available. The sale should be in the same condition as they are imported. Assessable Value is calculated by reducing post-importation costs and expenses from this selling price. This is called 'deductive value' because assessable value has to be arrived at by method of deduction (deduction means arrive at by inference i.e. by making suitable additions/subtractions from a known price to arrive at required 'Customs Value').

Price at or about the time of valuation - Price at or about the time at which goods in question are being valued should be considered. However, rule 7(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 provide that if such price is not available, price at the date after importation but within 90 days can be considered. Thus, if price prevalent prior to date of import of goods under-valuation is not available, even price subsequent to import of the goods can be considered under this rule.

Such sale should be in sufficient quantity to establish unit price.

Price after processing - If price of identical or similar goods in India is not available, but price in India is available after the imported goods are processed, such price can be considered after deducting processing cost. Such deduction should be on objective and quantifiable data. This method is not normally applicable if the imported goods lose identity after processing, unless value of imported component can be determined accurately without difficulty even after such conversion. This method also should not be applied if after processing, imported goods form a minor part of the processed goods. In such cases, reducing costs of other materials and processing costs from selling price of processed goods may not give reliable results [rule 7(3) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007].

The method may be used when goods are extracted on High Seas (e.g. minerals, crude oil etc.) and brought into India for sale. It will be 'import' and dutiable. In other cases, chances of using this method of valuation are indeed very rare.

Subtractions from selling price in India - Following subtractions should be made from selling price of imported goods in India. (a) Selling commission, general (selling) expenses and selling profits made in connection with sale of imported goods in India. General expenses includes direct and indirect cost of marketing the goods in question in India. (b) transport, insurance and associated costs within India (c) customs duties, sales tax and other taxes levied in India.

Seller in India of imported goods will incur all these expenses and hence, it is clear that 'CIF Value' can be arrived at i.e. 'deduced' only after all these expenses are reduced from selling price of identical or similar goods sold in India. In other words, all (estimated) expenses incurred after importation of goods should be subtracted from selling price in India to arrive at 'CIF Price' of goods.

Unit price sold in greatest numbers - Rule 7 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 specify that while considering selling price of imported goods in India, unit price at which greatest aggregate quantity of identical or similar goods are sold to unrelated persons in India should be the basis. Interpretative Note to rule 7 of Customs Valuation Rules gives some illustrations - e.g. if 65 units are sold @ Rs. 100, 55 units are sold @ Rs. 95 and 80 units are sold @ Rs. 90; then greatest aggregate quantity is 80 which is sold @ Rs. 90 per unit, which will be the basis for valuation. Another example given in the Interpretative Note is that if 500 units are sold at price of Rs. 95 and 400 units are sold at Rs. 90, then greatest quantity is 500 and hence price of Rs. 95 should be considered.
2005 taxmann.com 369 (Mumbai - CESTAT)[04-07-2005] Indian Oil Corpn. Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Customs, Ahmedabad

FACT: Appellants, manufacturers of glass sheets, charged from their customers the price of the goods as well as extra charges on account of special packing, cost of transport, forwarding charges, breakage risk and miscellaneous charges. The dispute was whether the charges for the extras were includible in the assessable value of the goods. When the same issue had gone to the High Court earlier, the appellants had contended that they realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers and not from their local buyers. The High Court held that as the appellants realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers, the extra charges were in principle excludible from the assessable value, and further, ordered the department of investigate the assertion of the facts made by the appellants. While the matter was under enquiry, the department received some information that the appellants were indulging in under-valuation of their goods. The Anti-Evasion staff of the department scrutinised the documents of the appellants and came to the conclusion that the appellants had highly inflated the costs of the extra items so as to camouflage the true assessable value of the goods. On this ground, show cause notices were issued demanding differential excise duty of Rs. 1,88,84,508.57 and also a penalty of Rs. 50 lakhs was imposed on the appellants for making false and mis-leading declarations. Confiscation of the plant and machinery of the appellants in lieu of a fine was also ordered. The appellants contended that the show-cause notices issued by the department were time-barred as they were issued beyond the normal time of six months. Further, the appellants pointed out that there has been a violation of principles of natural justice as their request to make further clarifications on the matter, was not honoured by the department. The question as to which of the items of extras should be held to be excludible for determining the assessable value of the goods was also taken up in the instant case.

HELD: As the assessment of the goods had been made only on a provisional basis, with the consent of the appellants, the demands as per the show cause notices are not time-barred. The limitation applies only from the date of adjustment of duty after finalisation of the provisional assessment "......the assessments had been made provisionally under Rule 9B of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 at their own request and on the strength of the provisional duty bond executed by them.......As per Rule 9B, the assessments made on provisional basis have to be finalised eventually and adjustments of duty made. Under Section 11A of the Act, the limitation starts running only from the date of adjustment of duty after finalisation of the provisional assessments. The demands issued as per the show cause notices on 6.11.1984, 10.12.1984 and 43.1985 were, therefore, not time barred, even if the normal time limit of six months were to be applied."

2. In not granting the appellants their request for a personal hearing wherein they wanted to make further submissions regarding certain points, the department has violated the principles of natural justice. "The appellants........argued their case in part and asked for certain clarifications. They expressed their desire to make further submissions on receipt.......The Collector did not grant this further hearing and he proceeded to decide the matter. There has, therefore, been a denial of full opportunity of personal hearing."

The TPO has no objection to the method of price analysis adopted by the assessee. There is no doubt that the assessee-company has entered into contracts of sale with its AE. After negotiations a contract price is agreed upon and the invoice is raised by the AE on the basis of that contract price. That contract price is comparable to the market rate available on the day of contract. Once the contract is entered into, the goods are moved from export destination to Kandla Port which is the import destination. Obviously, there is a time gap between the contract date and the date of entry. Because of this time gap between the contract date and entry date, there would be price fluctuation and the tariff rate furnished by the Customs need not be comparable to the price reflected in the import invoices. [Para 7]

As rightly argued by the assessee, instead of comparing the price with the customs tariff rate on the date of entry into the port, the TPO should have compared the price declared by the assessee with the customs tariff rate at Kandla Port as it is stood on the day of contract of sale entered into between the assessee and its AE. The TPO has not adopted this reasonable method. On the other hand, the TPO is going for customs tariff rate relevant for a subsequent date. This method is not a proper one. [Para 8]

There is no material on record to show that the price entered into between the parties on the date of contract was not comparable to similar transactions entered into on that day. It means that a price reflected in the sale contract entered into between the assessee and its AE is very much comparable to the market rate prevailing on that day. Therefore, compared to the illogical comparison made by the TPO, the price fixed by the parties on the basis of sale contract is more authentic and acceptable. The difference between the assessee's invoice rate and the average customs rate at Kandla Port is nominal. The difference goes beyond the permissible 5 per cent range only when the TPO has adopted the average of the tariff prices at Kandla Port. In these types of bulk purchases and sales, it is always better to compare the price of individual consignment rather than on a compromise of average price. [Para 9]

In the facts and circumstances of the case, there is no hard and fast reason to disturb the price disclosed by the assessee as the ALP for which the imports have been made. Therefore, the additional adjustment made by TPO is not sustainable in facts as well as in law. The addition is accordingly deleted. [Para 10]

The applicant is required to pay interest on the goods imported from E, Turkey, if there is delay in payment of more than 120 days from the date of the invoice, on the value of the goods. [Para 8]

On going through the provisions of section 7 it is found that as per section 7(2)(d), the activities to be treated as supply of goods or supply or services are covered in Schedule II. [Para 8.1] On going through the Schedule II, and comparing the same to the issue in hand, it is found that the foreign buyer has tolerated the act of receiving payment after a lapse of a period of 120 days from the date of the invoice in respect of the goods supplied by them to the applicant for which interest is to be paid by the applicant. Therefore, the aforementioned act will be covered under the Supply of Services under Entry No. 5(e) of the aforementioned Schedule II which reads as '(e) agreeing to the obligation to refrain from an act, or to tolerate an act or a situation, or to do an act'. However, since the payment of interest made by the applicant to the foreign buyer is connected to the goods imported by them and is with regard to the late payment of the value of goods imported by them from the foreign buyer, it is absolutely necessary to refer to section 15 which covers the valuation aspect in respect of supply of goods and services. [Para 8.2]

Section 15(2) pertains to all the things that shall be included in the value of supply. On going through the said sub-section, it is found that as per section 15(2)(d), value of supply also includes 'interest or late fee or penalty for delayed payment of any consideration for any supply.' Therefore, the payment of interest by the applicant will be covered under the supply of services under Entry No. 5(2)(e) of Schedule II and is liable to GST in view of the provisions of section 15(2)(d). [Para 8.3]

The interest paid by the applicant for delay in payment of the amount/value of the imported goods (paid after a lapse of a period of 120 days from the date of the invoice) is included as a part of the value of the said goods as per the provisions of section 15(2)(d). In view of the above, it is concluded that the rate of GST payable on the aforementioned interest will be the same as that of the IGST applicable on the aforementioned goods. [Para 8.4]

General Note :

Use of generally accepted accounting principles

1. "Generally accepted accounting principles" refers to the recognized consensus or substantial authoritative support within a country at a particular time as to which economic resources and obligations shall be recorded as assets and liabilities, which changes in assets and liabilities should be recorded, how the assets and liabilities and changes in them should be measured, what information should be disclosed and how it should be disclosed and which financial statements should be prepared. These standards may be broad guidelines of general application as well as detailed practices and procedures.

Notes to rules

Note to rule 2

In rule 2(2)(v), for the purposes of these rules, one person shall be deemed to control another when the former is legally or operationally in a position to exercise restraint or direction over the latter.

Note to rule 3

Price actually paid or payable

The price actually paid or payable is the total payment made or to be made by the buyer to or for the benefit of the seller for the imported goods. The payment need not necessarily take the form of a transfer of money. Payment may be made by way of letters of credit or negotiable instruments. Payment may be made directly or indirectly. An example of an indirect payment would be the settlement by the buyer, whether in whole or in part, of a debt owed by the seller.

Activities undertaken by the buyer on his own account, other than those for which an adjustment is provided in rule 10, are not considered to be an indirect payment to the seller, even though they might be regarded as of benefit to the seller. The costs of such activities shall not, therefore, be added to the price actually paid or payable in determining the value of imported goods.

The value of imported goods shall not include the following charges or costs, provided that they are distinguished from the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods :

(a) Charges for construction, erection, assembly, maintenance or technical assistance, undertaken after importation on imported goods such as industrial plant, machinery or equipment;

(b) The cost of transport after importation;

(c) Duties and taxes in India.

The price actually paid or payable refers to the price for the imported goods. Thus the flow of dividends or other payments from the buyer to the seller that do not relate to the imported goods are not part of the customs value.

Rule 3(2)(a)(iii)

Among restrictions which would not render a price actually paid or payable unacceptable are restrictions which do not substantially affect the value of the goods. An example of such restrictions would be the case where a seller requires a buyer of automobiles not to sell or exhibit them prior to a fixed date which represents the beginning of a model year.

Rule 3(2)(b)

If the sale or price is subject to some condition or consideration for which a value cannot be determined with respect to the goods being valued, the transaction value shall not be acceptable for customs purposes. Some examples of this include -

(a) The seller establishes the price of the imported goods on condition that the buyer will also buy other goods in specified quantities;

(b) the price of the imported goods is dependent upon the price or prices at which the buyer of the imported goods sells other goods to the seller of the imported goods;

(c) the price is established on the basis of a form of payment extraneous to the imported goods, such as where the imported goods are semifinished goods which have been provided by the seller on condition that he will receive a specified quantity of the finished goods.

However, conditions or considerations relating to the production or marketing of the imported goods shall not result in rejection of the transaction value. For example, the fact that the buyer furnishes the seller with engineering and plans undertaken in India shall not result in rejection of the transaction value for the purposes of rule 3. Likewise, if the buyer undertakes on his own account, even though by agreement with the seller, activities relating to the marketing of the imported goods, the value of these activities is not part of the value of imported goods nor shall such activities result in rejection of the transaction value.

Rule 3(3)

1. Rule 3(3)(a) and rule 3(3)(b) provide different means of establishing the acceptability of a transaction value.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: Storage cost is neither a cost of purchase nor of conversion nor can it be considered as toward bringing the inventory held in stock to its present location or condition. It is in the nature of a holding cost, which could be considered as an element of cost only where the goods have to be necessarily held in a particular manner, entailing cost, for a defined period, prior to their further processing, i.e., itself represents a process integral to their conversion, so that it represents a process and, thus, conversion cost. There is accordingly no question of the same being added to its value. A simple question would clarify the issue, i.e., whether rent, were the goods, instead of lying at the port, removed expeditiously to a rented premises, saving demurrage, or the cost of the staff attending thereto (godown) or otherwise supervising the storage, etc. be said to form part of the acquisition or conversion cost of the goods or otherwise incurred in bringing the same to their present location and condition, so as to be included in their valuation? Surely not. The third element of cost, i.e., other than toward acquisition and conversion, it would be noted, is broadly worded, so that it could in fact be said to include the cost of acquisition and conversion as well. It is only the direct cost incurred toward so bringing that could be included in as much as it adds value. In fact, the demurrage/detention charges, being toward the cost for the delay in removal of the goods, can only loosely/broadly be said to be a holding cost, and it would be more appropriate to consider it as a cost for the delayed removal of goods, i.e., beyond the stipulated period. The same thus is only a revenue expenditure of the period to which it relates and no more and, thus, not liable for inclusion in the value of the goods from any stand point.

As regards the objection by the revenue with reference to section 145A, the same deserves to fail. This is as even if the detention/demurrage charge is considered as not arising on account of a contractual obligation, but a statutory one, i.e., as in the nature of a levy or impost (which would though need to be established), it would stand to be included under section 145A only where it represents a qualifying cost - which have found as not, and not otherwise. ?

Definition of importer u/s 2(26) of Customs Act, 1962 ('CA, 1962') is proposed to be amended to include beneficial owner. Definition of 'beneficial owner' proposed to be included by inserting clause (3A) to Sec. 2 of CA, 1962 as under:

?

"Beneficial owner means any person on whose behalf the goods are being imported or exported or who exercises effective control over the goods being imported or exported".

?

The words 'effective control' is not defined under the CA, 1962. However Rule 2(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and Rule 2(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 defines that persons shall be deemed to be 'related' only if one of the conditions is satisfied. One of such condition under Rule 2(2)(v) is that one of them controls other directly or indirectly. Interpretative Note to Rule 2 clarify that for purpose of rule 2(2)(v), one person is deemed to control other if he is legally or operationally in a position to exercise restraint or direction over the other. Hence not just legal ownership but even operational control shall be sufficient to attract the provisions.

?

Applying said interpretation the words 'effective control' shall cover legal as well as operational control.

?

Said amendment has been proposed to cover those persons who use IEC of another to import goods and avoid the consequences because of some breach of law. One will also not be able to disown the goods on the ground of not being the owner.

CHARGES FOR LATE PRESENTATION OF BILL OF ENTRY

?

As per current Sec. 46(3) a bill of entry may be presented at any time after the delivery of the import manifest or import report as the case may be.

?

It is proposed by substituting existing Sec. 46(3) to provide that the bill of entry must be presented before the end of the next day following the day (excluding holidays) on which the aircraft or vessel or vehicle carrying the goods arrives at a customs station at which such goods are to be cleared for home consumption or warehousing. Without sufficient cause, importer shall be liable for charges for late presentation. Hence CHA's shall have to ensure that bill of entry is presented in time otherwise importer shall have to pay the charges for late presentation.

?

It may be noted that as per Sec. 15 of CA, 1962 the date of presentation of bill of entry is relevant date for determination of duty. However if a bill of entry has been presented before the date of entry inwards of the vessel or the arrival of the aircraft or the vehicle by which the goods are imported, the bill of entry shall be deemed to have been presented on the date of such entry inwards or the arrival, as the case may be.

?

Hon. CESTAT in the case of Sunrise Enterprise v. CCE [2015] 53 taxmann.com 321/49 GST 614 (New-Delhi – CESTAT) has held that an increase in anti-dumping duty after filing bill of entry cannot be made applicable as the date of presentation of bill of entry is the relevant date for determination of duty.

FACT: The appellants manufacture industrial gases, in their price list given to the Department they did not include handling charges (loading, unloading, transport etc.) and cylinder detention charges. These were recovered from customers by issuing debit notes and this was not declared before the authorities. After show cause proceedings, the Collector of Central Excise ordered that Rs. 10,15,798.19 ps. was to be paid by the petitioner for the period April, 1979 to February, 1984. A penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 was also imposed. Department also argued that the amount recovered as handling charges was far in excess of actual expenses incurred.

HELD: Limitation--extended 5 year period is applicable because as per the Rules, the appellants should have included handling and other charges upto factory gate in their price list. Hence penalty is also justified. "Filing of price lists is a statutory requirement. Accordingly we hold that there was suppression of facts on the part of the appellants and the extended period of limitation in terms of provisions of sub-section (1) of Section 11A of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 is applicable in this case. Consequently penalty on the appellants is also justified but in view of the fact that in succeeding paragraphs we are allowing deduction of some of the elements, we consider it fair to reduce the penalty to Rs. 50,000/- (Rupees fifty thousand only)."

2. Cylinder detention or rental being post-manufacturing expenses are not includible in assessable value. "...we hold that cylinder detention charges recovered by the appellants are not includible in the assessable value."

3. Handling and loading charges upto factory gate from part of assessable value, but similar expenses outside factory gate are not. "The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Assistant Collector of Central Excise and Others v. Madras Rubber Factory and Others reported in 1987 (27) ELT 553, 1987 (10) ECR--625 had held that the cost of distribution is not includible in case the whole-sale dealers take delivery of the goods from the outside duty-paid godowns. Accordingly the findings by the Collector that the handling charges incurred after the factory gate stage and recovered by the appellants are includible are set aside. However, the handling charges, if any incurred upto the factory gate stage would be includible in the assessable value.

4. Remand--Amount recovered in outside factory gate transactions, which are in excess of actual expenses incurred to be taken as part of the price realised by the appellant. Issue remanded for re-adjudication in the light of the above findings. "During the course of arguments the learned Jt. C.D.R. had argued that the amounts recovered from the customers under various heads were far in excess of the expenses actually incurred by the appellants on handling and unloading charges. We hold that the expenses actually incurred by the appellants on permissible deductions alone would be excludible and any excess recoveries from customers would be considered as part of the appellant's price realisation."

and accordingly the cost incurred by dealer towards PDI charges is not includible in assessable value. This view was further endorsed in the judgment of Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.v. Collector of Central Excise 1998 (103) E.L.T. 606 (New Delhi – Trib.) which was later on maintained by the Hon'ble Apex Court in Collectorv.Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. 1999 (111) E.L.T. A126. Post the Apex Court ruling in Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.'s case (supra), the CBEC issued a circular vide No. 681/72/2002-CX, dated 12-12-2002 clarifying that charges incurred by a dealer towards PDI and ASS activities will not be included in the transaction value. The earlier circulars issued in this regard stood withdrawn with the release of this circular.

Nearly after a decade when the issue of PDI and ASS seemed to have got settled, the judiciary again took the entire industry with a surprise when Delhi-CESTAT Larger Bench had given a contrary decision in the case of Maruti Suzuki India Ltd.v.CCE [2010] 1 taxmann.com 813. The Larger Bench of the Tribunal in its decision observed that every indirect benefit resulting from payment made by customers to a dealer in connection with or by reason of sale transaction is includible in the transaction value for levy of excise duty. Therefore, the amount collected by a dealer towards PDI or ASS from the buyer having understanding between manufacturer and dealer or forming part of sales promotion would be construed as payment to the dealer by buyer on behalf of the manufacturer and same is includible in the transaction value for levy of excise duty. The Larger Bench distinguished the ruling of Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.'s case (supra) on the basis that the dispute involved therein related to the period prior to the introduction of new valuation rules. The order passed by the Larger Bench was challenged by Maruti Suzuki in the Apex Court.

Post this decision of Delhi-CESTAT, the CBEC issued directions to field formations to decide all pending cases in light of the judgment pronounced in the matter of Maruti Suzuki India Ltd.'s case (supra).

In the meanwhile, the Bombay High Court in the matter of Tata Motors Ltd v. Union of India [2012] 25 taxmann.com 497/37 STT 140 has decided the issue in favour of the company. The Court observed that requirements of section 4(1)(a) of the CEA are complied as long as the manufacturer has sold the car to dealer with price as sole consideration, and both parties were not related to each other. In that view, these expenses were not includible in assessable value of car, as these were not paid by dealer to the manufacturer. The dealer has rendered these services as their legitimate activity, meeting labour cost for same from their retailing profit. These expenses were not covered in term 'servicing' mentioned in definition of 'transaction value'. Against this high court order, the department filed an appeal in Supreme Court.

However, after few months of Bombay high court ruling in Tata Motors Ltd.'s case (supra), the Apex Court dismissed the appeal filed in Maruti Suzuki India Ltd.'s case (supra) against the order of Delhi-CESTAT.

Recently, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of CCE v. TVS Motors Co. Ltd. [2015] 64 taxmann.com 261 has again turned the table in favour of the industry and held that cost of PDI and ASS borne by dealers from their profit margin would not be included in assessable value of manufacturer for levy of excise duty.

On appeal : HELD: From the case records, it was found that the assessee had collected various charges from importers/exporters including passengers for keeping the cargo in transit safely, pending export or customs clearance for home consumption. In holding that keeping safe custody of cargo in transit, pending clearance by the customs would constitute an activity exigible under the above entry, the lower authorities had relied on Circulars of the CBEC which clarified that storage and warehousing service provided by, inter alia, Airport Authority is covered by the entry. The entry cargo handling service was clarified by the CBEC as not covering export cargo and passenger baggage. The clarification was not to the effect that all activities relating to export cargo and passenger baggage were also excluded from levy under other entries. The finding of the Commissioner, that the exceptions provided under cargo handling services with regard to passenger baggage and export cargo could not be claimed under storage and warehousing services, was to be agreed with. [Para 9.2]

Demurrage or wharfage charges were collected, respectively, in relation to clearance of import/export cargo beyond five days and 24 hours. As found by the original authority, these were higher charges for continued storage of cargo collected by the assessee from members of the trade. These were part of the taxable value collected towards storage and warehouse charges. [Para 9.3]

As regards the abandoned cargo, those accrued to the assessee towards storage and warehousing of cargo, which were not taken delivery of by the importer. The procedure for auctioning abandoned cargo and the sharing of the proceeds is prescribed by the Ministry of Finance. These instructions also make it clear that the assessee would receive amounts towards the service of storage and warehousing of cargo under this head. However, the services were not rendered to any person in the case of the abandoned cargo. Therefore, demand under this head was not sustainable. [Para 9.4]

As regards the destination charges, it was found that the assessee had collected the documents representing the consignments brought by Air India and Blue Dart and hand over these to the respective consignees. In cases where the assessee merely collected and handed over the documents to the respective consignees, destination charges would not form part of taxable value under storage and warehousing. [Para 9.5]

As regards the OT charges/penalties, the lower authorities had not given a finding as to the nature and purpose of these penalties but had presumed that these were collected for violations on the part of their clients in relation to storage and warehousing services. The Commissioner (Appeals) did not find this item to be taxable under storage and warehousing. In the absence of a finding as to how that amount was taxable towards any service rendered by the assessee, it was difficult to accept the stand of the revenue in this regard. The assessee had also not explained the nature and purpose of collecting these charges. This matter would be decided after hearing the party afresh. [Para 9.6]

CUSTOM HOUSE AGENT’S SERVICE

V.S. DATEY

VALUATION OF CHA SERVICE : CBE&C CIRCULAR SOLVES SOME PROBLEMS, BUT CREATES MORE PROBLEMS

CBE&C, vide Circular No. 119/13/2009-ST, dated December 21, 2009, has clarified some issues relating to valuation of Customs House Agent’s (CHA) services. Surprisingly, the circular is conceptually very clear on many issues (such circulars are nowadays rare). However, the view that CHA should recover reimbursements on ‘actual’ basis and if there is any mark up or margin, entire charges (and not the mark up alone) will be included in the taxable value, is highly controversial and litigation prone. The view does not seem to be correct in the author’s opinion. The view that there should be agreement between customer and CHA may also be a source of disputes and litigation.

Nature of services provided by CHA

1. As per section 65(105 )(h) of the Finance Act, 1994, any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a custom house agent in relation to the entry or departure of conveyances or the import or export of goods, is a ‘taxable service’.

Thus, services of CHA in relation to entry/departure of conveyances or import/export of goods are taxable. The CBE&C, vide Circular No. 119/13/2009-ST, dated December 21, 2009 has correctly clarified that activities of CHA pertain to customs formalities in relation to the entry or departure of conveyance or the import or export of goods. These (only these) are subject to service tax.

1.1 Other expenses incurred by CHA and recovered from customer - All work within the customs area is handled by CHA as others do not have easy access to these areas. The CHA hires various services on behalf of customer and pays for the same. Often bill of service provider (e.g., transporter, cargo handler, packer, warehouse-keeper, port trust) is in name of CHA and not in name of ultimate customer. The CHA recovers value of these services from customer usually with markup, i.e., by adding his own margin.

As per para 2 of the CBE&C Circular No. 119/13/2009-ST, dated December 21, 2009, the following services can be treated as not part of CHA services and will not be includible in ‘value’ for payment of service tax on CHA services, if recovered from customer on actual basis - (a) packing and unpacking (b) loading and unloading and (c) bringing or removing goods from customs area, vessels or aircrafts for the customers (importer or exporter). These services are provided by various agencies like port trust, steamer agents, cargo handlers, warehouse-keepers, packers, goods transport agents. Similar arrangement can be for payment of statutory duties like customs duties, port charges, cesses, etc.

1.2 Conditions for not including these charges in the taxable value of CHA service - These charges will not be includible in taxable value of CHA service for payment of service tax if conditions as specified in para 6 of the CBE&C Circular dated December 21, 2009 are satisfied. The conditions are - (a) Activity should be in addition to CHA service, (b) There should be agreement between customer and CHA, (c) CHA does not use activities/services for his own benefit, (d) CHA should recover reimbursements on actual basis, (e) CHA should provide nexus between other (than CHA) services and the reimbursable amount. Invoice need not be in name of ultimate customer, (f) The charge by CHA to customer should be either by separate invoice or separate entry in a common invoice, (g) Any miscellaneous or out of pocket expenses will be considered part of CHA services and will be includible in taxable value.

Basically, these are conditions of ‘pure agent’ as specified in the Service Tax Valuation Rules.

FACT: By review order under Section 35(b) CESA, the Collector added Rs. 9472.95 to the assessable value of the appellants who are manufacturers of metal containers, on the ground that they charged from customers freight at a higher rate than declared. Longer period of limitation was also invoked.

HELD: I Minority view per Member (J)]: Valuation--Unloading charges outside factory gate are not includible in the assessable value. As regards loading charges within the factory, there is no specific charge in the show cause notice. It refers to freight, which is also not includible in the assessable value. (Ratio of Indian Oxygen Ltd. v. CCE Bombay Tyre International). "There is no specific charge that they have charged loading/unloading charges at higher rates than declared. It is only the Collector who says that the appellants charged loading and unloading charges at a particular rate. According to the decision of the Supreme Court........unloading charges outside the factory-gate are not includible in the assessable value. Therefore, the question of mis-declaration as regards the inclusion of unloading charges outside the factory-gate falls to the ground. As regards the inclusion of loading charges within the factory-gate, the charge in this show cause is vague. It refers to freight. According to Bombay Tyre International..........freight is not includible in the assessable value. According to the language used in the show cause notice, the entire charge of charging freight at a higher rate falls to the ground in view of the Bombay Tyre International However, taking into account the order of the Collector, the loading within the factory is includible. As stated earlier, there is no specific allegation to this effect in the show cause notice."

Limitation--Before the judgment of the Supreme Court in Indian Oxygen case (1988) the question of includibility of loading charges incurred within the factory was not clear and the law was in a fluid state. As such, the charge of misdeclaration when the legal position itself is not clear is like charging the appellants in vacuum. The show cause notice is, therefore, barred by limitation. "Till the judgment of the Supreme Court in the Indian Oxygen case, the decision as to the includibility of loading charges within the factory is not clear and law was in a fluid state. In Bombay Tyre International, it is not specifically stated that loading charges within the factory is to be included although it was categorically observed that the expenses incurred upto the factory-gate cannot be deducted from the assessable value. Therefore, to charge the manufacturer with mis-declaration when legal position itself is not clear is like charging him in vacuum. Therefore, we are of the view that the show cause notice is barred by limitation. Accordingly, we allow the appeal and set aside the order of the lower authority on grounds that the show cause notice is barred by limitation. The appeal is, thus, allowed."

[Majority view per Member (T) Vice-President]: Valuation--The appellants admittedly collected transportation charges, be it for loading, unloading or handling the barrels. Of these, the charges incurred on loading and handling of goods within the factory are required to be included in the assessable value, according to the Supreme Court's judgment in Indian Oxygen Ltd For determining such charges, the case is remanded to the Asstt. Collector. There is thus an admission on the part of the appellants that the so-called transportation charges 'or delivery charges', whatever the name was given to them by the appellants included some charges towards loading within the factory on the wagons, trucks, etc from the stacking place after the manufacture of barrels and metal containers. This being the position and in view of the Supreme Court's judgment in the case of Indian Oxygen Ltd. v. CCE. expenses incurred towards the loading of the goods within the factory are required to be included in the assessable value of the goods Since a separate break-up of these charges is not given out of the total transportation cost or delivery charges collected by the assessee from its customers, the case has necessarily to be remanded for determining the charges collected towards loading and handling of the goods within the factory for the purpose of charging duty thereon and I order accordingly."

In VST Industries Ltd.14, the honorable Supreme Court has distinguished Metal Box decision by observing that the notional interest on interest free deposit made by the buyer to the seller should not be included in the sale price of the seller-Assessee as no extra commercial consideration is flowing from the buyer to the seller, there is no nexus between the security deposit and sale price, and if department is not able to quantify the money value of the additional consideration.

The position is completely different from present regime. Section 67 of Service Tax doesn't provide for such inclusion.15

EU directive has no similar provision.

Subsidies

The CGST Act in sub clause (e) provides-

(e) subsidies directly linked to the price excluding subsidies provided by the Central Government and State Governments.

Explanation.––For the purposes of this sub-section, the amount of subsidy shall be included in the value of supply of the supplier who receives the subsidy.

If any subsidies received by supplier linked to supply than its need to be added in the "Transaction value" however, general subsidy are not required to be added in the transaction value. The subsidy received is not in connection with or by reason of sale of goods is not an additional consideration.

In Maruti Case16, the Assessee retained with it 50% of sales tax collected from its customers and it was neither actually paid to exchequer nor was it actually payable to exchequer .That being position, transaction value was required to be calculated by including amount retained by Assessee.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court's decision in the case of Mazagon Dock Ltd17 saying that the subsidy has been received subsequent to clearance of goods and has no connection with the value of the DDT manufactured and sold.

In TISCO General Office Recreation Club case18 the subsidy was given by the TISCO to TISCO club which provided food to the employees and issue was whether this subsidy amount received by the club is also liable to tax in the hands of club. Supreme Court held that since it is not relatable to any particular item, it cannot become a sale price i.e. it is not part of the turnover and accordingly no tax is payable on the said amount. Reiterated again by Tribunal.19

The position of law has changed as the Excise Act, specifically excludes subsidy. Further in reference to sales tax, the same must have direct connection to particular item.

Article 73 of EU directive20 provides for inclusion subsidies directly linked to the price of supply. Thus, position is same under CGST like EU directive with exception regarding certain subsidies.

Not to be Included

The CGST Act in Section 15(3) provides that discount of particular type to be not included in value.

(3) The value of the supply shall not include any discount which is given––

(a)

before or at the time of the supply if such discount has been duly recorded in the invoice issued in respect of such supply; and

(b)

iable and liable to customs duty or excise duty". Section 18(a) of the Singapore GST Act specifies that the value of imported goods for the purpose of levy of GST should be the aggregate of the value determined in terms of section 22 of the Singapore Customs Act and the customs duties and other taxes excluding GST levied, if any, on such imports. In the absence of such a reference to the Customs Act, 1962 in the IGST Act, an importer is faced with – Having to negotiate and apply two sets of valuation rules - one prescribed by the Customs Act for the purpose of levy of the Customs duties and another prescribed by the GST Valuation (Determination of the Value of Supply of Goods and Services) Rules, 2016 (hereinafter also referred to as the GST Valuation Rules) for the levy of IGST. The two sets of valuation rules, though similar are not identical. For instance, the GST Valuation Rules similar to the Customs Valuation Rules, do provide for acceptance of transaction value, even if the transaction is between related parties, provided the relationship has not influenced the price. However, unlike the Customs Valuation Rules, the GST Valuation Rules do not provide the method by which the importer can demonstrate that the relationship has not influenced the price and, therefore, the transaction value has to be accepted. Further, one other major difference is that the GST Valuation Rules, unlike the Customs Valuation Rules, do not contain the "Deductive/Sale Minus/Transaction Net Margin (TNMM) method" of valuation. This means that importers who import goods from related parties, especially traders/re-sellers who traditionally rely on the Deductive Method to value their goods or use it to demonstrate that the transaction is at arms' length for the customs valuation would be left in a quandary, as they cannot use this method to arrive at the Value for the purpose of levy of IGST.

There is a lack of clarity on the timing and procedure to pay IGST. Would IGST be levied and collected by the Customs authorities at the time of import together with Customs duties or should it be paid on reverse charge1 basis post-import in the same manner as is applicable to other reverse charge supplies of goods?

Apart from the issues that we have already discussed in the foregoing paragraphs, section 29(1)(b) of the Model Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2016 appears to suggest that input tax credit is available on customs duties paid under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. What does this mean in a GST regime? Does it mean Additional Duties of Customs would continue to be levied under GST regime or does it mean that section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act would be amended to reflect IGST instead of the Additional Duties currently levied? There is a disconnection between the IGST Act and the Customs Tariff Act, both of which attempt to levy IGST on imports. There is not enough information to form an opinion on the questions posed and, as such, we would refrain from making any, suffice to bring out the areas where more information/clarity is required.

Concluding Remarks

3. We hope that the Union Government would work on these aspects and make the necessary amendments to the IGST Act and the GST Valuation Rules before the enactment/introduction of the GST regime in line with international practice, else it is bound to cause needless hardships and avoidable litigations to the importers as well as to the field formations administering the GST Acts.

When the duty of excise is chargeable with reference to the value of goods, section 4 provides that on each removal of the goods, the value will be determined either under clause (a) or clause (b).

Section 4 yields the following elements:

Apart from what is shown as the price the transaction value would include:

Any amount the buyer is liable to pay to the assessee by reason of or in connection with the sale whether at the time of the sale or any other time.

Thus the intent is to determine the value by not only including the actual price paid or payable but all amounts which are separately enumerated. [Para 16]

Rule 4 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 falls under the heading 'duty payable on removal'. It is contemplated that duty is to be paid on the goods in the manner provided under rule 8 or under any law. No excisable good on which duty is payable can be removed without payment of excise duty unless otherwise provided. Rule 8 under the heading 'manner of payment' declares that duty on the goods removed from the factory, etc. during a month shall be paid by the 5th day of the following month. Removal, however, in the month of March will entail liability to pay by 31st day of March. Sub-rule (3) of rule 8 provides for liability with the assessee who fails to pay the amount by the due date. Sub-rule (4) refers to liability to pay interest. It is amply clear that the expression 'due date' would be 5th day of the month following the month during which the goods are removed except with regard to the goods removed during the month of March in which case the due date would be 31st day of March. [Para 17]

The Scheme of the Rules further is that assessment is to be done by the assessee itself by way of self-assessment and the duty paid by the due date. What is to happen when the assessee is confronted with a situation when it is unable to determine the value of the goods or find the rate of duty. Rule 7 provides the solution. The assessee can thereunder apply giving reasons and seeking permission to make a provisional assessment. The Officer may grant such permission. Thereupon duty is payable on a provisional basis. The value or the rate would be indicated by the Officer in the order permitting such provisional assessment. This is, however, made subject to the assessee executing a bond binding the assessee to pay the difference between the duty as payable under the final assessment and the provisional assessment. The final assessment is to be made within six months from the date of communication of the order permitting provisional assessment under rule 7(1). The period can be extended by the Commissioner for six months and by the Chief Commissioner for which there is no time limit.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 7 provides as follows:

(1)

The assessee shall be liable to pay interest.

(2)

On any amount payable based on a final assessment under rule 7(3).

(3)

At the rate fixed under section 11A or section 11B of the Act.

(4)

From the first date of the month succeeding the month for which the amount is determined till the date of payment thereof.

Rule 7(5) contemplates interest on refund based on the final assessment. [Para 18]

While levy of interest is a part of the adjective law, yet to levy interest there must be substantive provision. Demand for interest can be made only if the legislature has specifically intended collection of interest. [Para 22]

V S DATEY

Background

Corruption in any department of Government is nothing new. Customs department is no exception [Of course this does not mean that there is no corruption in private sector, but there public at large is not the sufferer]. Reference to corruption in customs department are found even in Kautilya's writings. Let us be honest and say that people have accepted corruption as way of life. It is treated as 'lubricant' in doing business.

However, presently, in customs, it is not only a 'lubricant' but is tending towards 'rape'. This really hurts common importers and exporters. [Uncommon businessmen have their own way of doing things. Let us not count them].

One such tool of harassment in customs is 'Special Valuation Branch' (SVB). Luckily, this has been realized by CBE&C and SVB has been cut to size. The revised provisions relating to SVB as contained in CBE&C Circular No. 5 /2016 -Cus dated 9-2-2016 are discussed in the Article.

Purpose of SVB is to examine related party transactions

Related party transactions are almost always treated with suspicion in all tax laws including income tax, excise and customs.

The 'Special Valuation Branch' (SVB) was created as an institution in customs in 1998, specializing in investigation of transactions involving special relationships between buyer - seller or those involving other special circumstances surrounding the sale of imported goods. Both of these have a bearing on the assessable value.

Detailed instructions were issued vide Circular Nos. 1/1998-Cus dated 1-1-1998 and 11/2001-Cus dated 23-2-2001 in respect of SVB. This resulted in continued uncertainty due to provisional assessments, increase in transaction costs and burdensome procedure of renewal of SVB orders [These are not my words. These are words of CBE&C itself].

In the meanwhile, WCO (World Customs Organisation) has issued Guide to Customs Valuation and Transfer Pricing in June 2015. Hence, provisions relating to SVB have been revamped vide CBE&C Circular No. 5 /2016 -Cus dated 9-2-2016.

SVB will be under supervisory control of jurisdictional customs officers

Since 1-1-2013, functional control over SVBs was with the Director General of Valuation (DGOV). Now, SVB will be under supervisory control of jurisdictional Chief Commissioner/Principal Commissioner/Commissioner.

DGoV shall now only support the SVBs by issuing advisories on legal issues & guidance notes. DGoV shall also continue to qualitatively monitor investigation orders issued by SVBs.

The system of renewal of SVB orders has been discontinued with immediate effect.

Jurisdiction of SVB is where corporate office of importer is situated

The SVBs are presently functioning at the Customs Houses at Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi and Mumbai. Jurisdiction of the SVBs will be based upon the principle of location of the corporate office of the importer. As andwhen imports requiring investigation by SVBs are noticed at any customs formation, the concerned Commissionerate shall transfer all relevant records to the jurisdictional SVB for investigations. However, where the import takes place through CHs of Mumbai / Delhi / Chennai / Kolkata / Bangalore, the importer will be free to select the SVB of the Customs House of import or the Customs House most proximate to the corporate office, as convenient to him.

Abolition of Extra Duty Deposit of 1%

At present, during investigation by SVB, 'Extra Duty Deposit' (EDD) @ 1% of declared assessable value is obtained from the importer for a period of 4 months during which time he is required to submit required documents and information to the SVB. However, in practice, the 1% EDD continues till completion of investigation. Obtaining refund is very cumbersome.

Hence, now, in case of cases referred to SVB, the assessment will be provisional on basis of Provisional Duty (PD) bond, but EDD will not be required.

However, if the importer fails to provide documents and information required for SVB inquiries, within 60 days of such requisition, security deposit at a rate of 5% of the declared assessable value shall be imposed by the Commissioner for a period not exceeding the next three months. Simultaneously, the importer shall be granted a further period of 60 days to comply with the requisition for information & documents. If the importer fails to submit documents within this extended period, the Commissioner in charge of SVB may consider the use of other provisions of the Customs Act for obtaining documents / information from an importer for conducting investigations.

In no case shall the imposition of Security Deposit exceed the period of three months specified above.

FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of pig iron.

During the period June 1998 to August 1998, the assessee imported Low Ash Metallurgical (LAM) Coke under seven Bills of Entry, against four advance licenses without payment of —

basic customs duty (BCD) levied under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962,

special customs duty (SCD) levied under section 68 of the Finance Act, 1996,

special additional duty (SAD) levied under section 3A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and

anti-dumping duty (ADD) levied under section 9A of Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

The department sought to deny exemptions on failure to fulfil export obligation.

Pending final adjudication of notice by the Commissioner, the assessee duly paid the entire duty payable towards BCD, SAD and SCD after considering partial exports already made. The assessee did not make any payment towards ADD.

The department confirmed duty demands along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent as per bond.

Tribunal enhanced ADD as per revised notification but reduced interest to 15 per cent.

The assessee challenged Anti-dumping duty, interest and penalty and other computations.

Assessee's Arguments

Basic customs duty and the special customs duty as well as special additional duty was payable by the assessee.

However, anti-dumping duty was not payable at all, as assessee was exempt under Notification No. 69 of 2000.

Notification No. 30 of 1997 did not stipulate that in the event of default, interest would become payable; hence, interest was not payable.

Since assessment was provisional, there was no provision for collection of interest for the period in dispute as section 18 was amended to include such a provision only prospectively with effect from 2006.

In any case, Anti-dumping duty could not be added for purposes of computing customs duty, special customs duty and special additional duty.

Also no penalty is imposable inasmuch as nothing contumacious was done by the assessee and the export obligation could not be fulfilled only because of bona fide commercial impossibility.

Since appeal before Tribunal was filed by assessee, he could not be worse off in an appeal filed only by the assessee herein to CESTAT and that on the assumption that the assessee was liable to pay anti-dumping duty, they should only pay the said duty at the lower rate prescribed by the Commissioner as revenue had not appealed to the Tribunal against the Commissioner's order.

Revenue's Arguments

The exemption contained in Anti-dumping duty Notification 69 of 2000 was only prospective and, hence Anti-dumping duty had to be paid for the relevant period.

Interest was payable as Notification No. 30 of 1997 independently levied a charge of interest.

Order of Tribunal was correct in law.

5. As per rule 6(2)(iv) of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, the value of any taxable service, as the case may be, does not include interest on delayed payment of any consideration for the provision of services or sale of property, whether movable or immovable.

provided by Government or a local authority

to a business entity

Thus, if government has provided any taxable service to business entity and payment therefor is allowed to be deferred on payment of interest or other charges, then, such interest or other charges shall, apparently, form part of the value of the services.

5.1 Exclusion from exclusion : One would wonder whether interest for belated payment towards 'service' is a consideration for providing 'service' so as to be includible in value. 5.2 Whether in negative list under Section 66D(n) : Section 66D(n)(i) covers within negative list, services by way of extending deposits, loans or advances in so far as the consideration is represented by way of interest or discount. This section has been interpreted by CBEC Education Guide as follows :

4.14.2 What are the "services by way of extending deposits, loans or advances in so far as the consideration is represented by way of interest or discount"?

The negative list entry covers any such service wherein moneys due are allowed to be used or retained on payment of interest or on a discount. The words used are 'deposits, loans or advances and have to be taken in the generic sense. They would cover any facility by which an amount of money is lent or allowed to be used or retained on payment of what is commonly called the time value of money which could be in the form of an interest or a discount. This entry would not cover investments by way of equity or any other manner where the investor is entitled to a share of profit.

Illustrations of such services are –

Fixed deposits or saving deposits or any other such deposits in a bank or a financial institution for which return is received by way of interest.

Providing a loan or overdraft facility or a credit limit facility in consideration for payment of interest.

Mortgages or loans with a collateral security to the extent that the consideration for advancing such loans or advances are represented by way of interest.

Corporate deposits to the extent that the consideration for advancing such loans or advances are represented by way of interest or discount.
