The assessment was framed on a provisional basis including the cost of free PDI and ASS in the transaction value for levy of excise duty. The assessee filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) against the order which was allowed and the case was remanded back. The department filed an appeal against the order before the CESTAT which was also rejected. The matter went to the Apex Court for consideration. The Apex Court looked into the detailed history of litigations and provisions applicable prior to year 2000 and post 2000 when the new valuation rules were introduced. The Apex Court placed reliance on several decisions and in-particular the decision in the case of Philips India Ltd.v. Collector of Central Excise 1997 taxmann.com 1239 wherein deduction of the cost incurred towards advertisement expenses and free ASS during guarantee period provided by dealers to the product of Philips under agreement was allowed. The court also placed reliance on the judgment of this vary court in the case of Commissioner v.Telco Ltd. 2001 (130) ELT A260 (SC), wherein the Apex Court has affirmed the view of the Tribunal holding that when goods are sold to independent dealers at arm's length, payment directly made by the manufacturer for labour ASS to additional service centres arranged by the manufacturer and subsequent recovery of such expenses by the manufacturer from the dealer, is not a case of flow-back of additional consideration nor does such an arrangement make such dealer an agent of the assessee.

Placing reliance on the above judicial precedents, the Apex Court held that PDI and ASS charges would not be included in the assessable value under section 4 of the Act for the purposes of paying excise duty. The Apex Court observed that where manufacturer himself does the ASS and incurs any expenditure thereon, the same is not deductible from the price charged by him from his buyer. However, where the manufacturer has sold his goods to his dealer and wholesale dealer thereafter does ASS to the customer and incurs expenditure therefore, it cannot be added back to the sale price charged by the manufacturer from the dealer for computing the assessable value. This is more so, where the ASS is done by the dealer many weeks after the goods have been sold to him by the manufacturer. Such a post-sale activity undertaken by the dealer is not relevant for the purpose of excise since the goods have already been marketed to the dealer.

The Apex Court overruled the judgment of Larger Bench in Maruti Suzuki India Ltd.'s case (supra) and quashed the circulars which provided for inclusion of PDI and ASS charges in the assessable/transaction value for levy of excise duty.

Comments

5. The judgment of Apex Court has put to rest the long drawn ambiguity in the matter pertaining to inclusion of PDI and ASS in the transaction/assessable value. It is noteworthy that this ruling puts to rest the ambiguity that got erupted again in the backdrop of legislative developments made vide amendment in section 4 of CEA which defined 'transaction value' as price actually paid or payable by the buyer including additional amount that the buyer is liable to pay or on behalf of the assessee by reason of sale or in connection of sale whether payable at the time of sale or at any other time including the amount charged for or to make provision for certain items such as advertising, servicing etc.

Conclusion

6. In light of the recent Apex Court ruling restoring the old thought process with respect to non-inclusion of cost of PDI and ASS borne by the dealer in the transaction/assessable value for levy of excise duty, the automobile industry might just find a ray of hope at the end of the tunnel.

This judgment is certainly a push back to the department after the admission of their Special Leave Petition by Hon'ble Apex Court against the order of Bombay High Court in Tata Motors Ltd.'s case (supra). However, considering the history wherein we have seen the law being amended to nullify decisions of Apex Court to prevail department's view, it will be no surprise that the Government in the ensuing budget may make necessary amendments in section 4 of the CEA to bring back the taxability of PDI and ASS within the ambit of transaction value which may again start a new array of controversies in this matter.

As we know, India is on the verge of a change in indirect tax regime from present complex tax structure to more simplified Goods and Services Tax regime. At this juncture, it is important for Government to take note of such issues and have clear guidelines to avoid possible litigation on such aspects under the proposed GST regime.

(1) Whether Section 145A overrides the provisions of Section 36(1)(iii)?

The proviso to section 36(1)(iii) incorporated in Part D of Chapter IV of the Act providing for the 'Method of Computation of Total Income', will override provisions of section 145A, which is incorporated in Chapter IV of the Act relating to 'procedure for assessment'. The words in the proviso to section 36(1) 'whether capitalised or not' will override the accounting practice followed in the books of account by the assessee. In the present case, the assessee has admittedly capitalised the interest paid on the borrowed capital. The assesse also did not claim that the land in question was put to use in the assessment years in question. Mere purchase of the land in the years in question out of the borrowed capital does not entitle the assessee to claim such interest paid on borrowed capital as a deductible expenditure in the present assessment years merely on the basis of method of accounting prescribed under section 145A which was brought in the statute to undo the effect of the decision of the Delhi High Court in Chamber of Tax Consultants v. Union of India [2017] 87 taxmann.com 92 [2018] 252 Taxman 77/400 ITR 178 (Delhi) which quashed the CBDT Notification No. 87 of 2016 dated 29.9.2016 finding it to be ultra vires. The method of accounting provided for the valuation of inventory under section 145A does not determine the allowability of the expenditure. The proviso to section 36(1)(iii), which says that such a claim of deduction will be allowed in the assessment years when it was put to use, will override the provisions contained in section 145A. (2) Is it necessary to add customs duty (not yet paid) to the value of imported materials kept at customs bonded warehouse?

According to section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962, customs duty shall be levied on goods imported into or exported from India. Section 2(23) of the said Act defines 'import' as bringing into India from a place outside India. Section 2(27) of the said Act defines India as including the territorial waters of India. Therefore, the taxable event occurs when goods enter the territorial waters of India. Duty liability has arisen but is only deferred by deposit in the bonded warehouse. Deposit in the bonded warehouse does not extinguish the duty liability. Therefore, the duty element should be added for making the adjustments under section 145A. ["Issues on Tax Audit" by ICAI]

(3) Is a Deposit made with port trust in the nature of the tax, duty, cess or fee liable to be added under Section 145A to the cost of imports?

The deposit made with the port trust is not includible in the computation made under section 145A, if it does not fall in the category of tax, duty, cess or fee levied under any law. Hence, the same shall be liable to be included in the adjustments made under section 145A only if it is shown that the payment was made under the authority of any law. Adjudication by customs officer and not by SVB

The SVB shall convey its investigative findings by way of an Investigation Report to the referring customs formation for finalizing the provisional assessments. Thus, assessment order will be issued by jurisdictional customs officer and not by SVB.

Commissioner to decide whether case is to be referred to SVB

Importer will submit a questionnaire duly filled in, in prescribed form to the jurisdictional Commissioner. On the basis of the information, Commissioner will take a decision on whether a case needs to be referred to SVB for investigations.

Only cases with significant revenue implications should be taken up for SVB investigations. Hence, the following cases shall not be taken up for inquiries by SVBs - (i) Import of samples and prototypes from related sellers (ii) Imports from related sellers where duty chargeable (including additional duty of Customs etc.) is unconditionally fully exempted or nil (iii) Any transaction where the value of imported goods is less than Rs 1 lakhs but cumulatively these transactions do not exceed Rs 25 lakhs in any financial year.

Cases which may be considered for SVB Investigations

While filing a bill of entry, every importer makes a declaration about whether the seller of imported goods is a related party or not, as defined under Rule 2(2) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 (CVR, 2007). Such transactions will require to be examined as to whether SVB inquiries are necessary.

Further, transactions where any payments are sought to be made which are in the nature of instances given below, shall be examined with respect to the need for SVB investigations:(a)'royalty and license fee' under Rule 10 (1)(c) of CVR, 2007 or(b)where the value of any part of proceeds of any subsequent resale, disposal or use of imported goods accrues to the seller under Rule (10)(1)(d) of CVR, 2007 or (c) where any other payments are made or are contemplated to be made in future by buyer to seller as a condition of sale of imported goods etc. under Rule 10(1)(e)of CVR, 2007.

No reference to SVB would be necessary where any additions are sought to be made under Clauses (a) and (b) of Rule 10(1), as such matters would be decided routinely by Appraising Groups.

Procedure for considering reference to SVB

At the time of first imports from related party, the importer should file Advance Bill of Entry and also information as prescribed.

On the basis of such information, the proper officer of customs will determine whether, prima facie, there is a need for investigation by the SVB. He shall complete such examination within 3 days of the filing of Bill of Entry and the matter submitted before the Commissioner.

The Commissioner of Customs shall after due consideration of the preliminary findings, take a considered view whether the matter should be referred to SVB or not.

Procedure for reference to SVB

In the event of the Commissioner directing investigations by SVB, the proper officer of customs shall promptly carry out provisional assessment in terms of section 18 of the Customs Act, 1962 and ensure that no delays occur in the release of the goods.

The proper officer will also ask for further information as specified in Annexure B to the CBE&C circular. The importer will be advised to furnish the documents and a duly indexed reply to the questionnaire to the jurisdictional SVB within 60 days.

After completion of the procedure for provisional assessment and issue of the questionnaire, all related records shall be transferred to the jurisdictional SVB, within 3 working days of the release of the goods.

Once documents are submitted, provisional assessments, without security deposit or bank guarantee, continue till the finalisation of the investigation.

Procedure for cases where reference to SVB is not required

Where it is decided by the Commissioner of customs that a reference to SVB is not necessary, the Customs House shall issue a reference number to the importer and the Risk Management Division to indicate that the transaction has been examined from the point of view of need for SVB inquiries and it has been decided not to refer the same for SVB investigations.

FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of pig iron.

During the period June 1998 to August 1998, the assessee imported Low Ash Metallurgical (LAM) Coke under seven Bills of Entry, against four advance licenses without payment of —

basic customs duty (BCD) levied under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962,

special customs duty (SCD) levied under section 68 of the Finance Act, 1996,

special additional duty (SAD) levied under section 3A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and

anti-dumping duty (ADD) levied under section 9A of Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

The department sought to deny exemptions on failure to fulfil export obligation.

Pending final adjudication of notice by the Commissioner, the assessee duly paid the entire duty payable towards BCD, SAD and SCD after considering partial exports already made. The assessee did not make any payment towards ADD.

The department confirmed duty demands along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent as per bond.

Tribunal enhanced ADD as per revised notification but reduced interest to 15 per cent.

The assessee challenged Anti-dumping duty, interest and penalty and other computations.

Assessee's Arguments

Basic customs duty and the special customs duty as well as special additional duty was payable by the assessee.

However, anti-dumping duty was not payable at all, as assessee was exempt under Notification No. 69 of 2000.

Notification No. 30 of 1997 did not stipulate that in the event of default, interest would become payable; hence, interest was not payable.

Since assessment was provisional, there was no provision for collection of interest for the period in dispute as section 18 was amended to include such a provision only prospectively with effect from 2006.

In any case, Anti-dumping duty could not be added for purposes of computing customs duty, special customs duty and special additional duty.

Also no penalty is imposable inasmuch as nothing contumacious was done by the assessee and the export obligation could not be fulfilled only because of bona fide commercial impossibility.

Since appeal before Tribunal was filed by assessee, he could not be worse off in an appeal filed only by the assessee herein to CESTAT and that on the assumption that the assessee was liable to pay anti-dumping duty, they should only pay the said duty at the lower rate prescribed by the Commissioner as revenue had not appealed to the Tribunal against the Commissioner's order.

Revenue's Arguments

The exemption contained in Anti-dumping duty Notification 69 of 2000 was only prospective and, hence Anti-dumping duty had to be paid for the relevant period.

Interest was payable as Notification No. 30 of 1997 independently levied a charge of interest.

Order of Tribunal was correct in law.

Valuation under GST 4. It is pertinent to note that, though taxability of the said ocean freight service is quite clear under GST regime, yet there may be certain doubts on the method of valuation to be adopted for levying IGST on such ocean freight. Unlike the erstwhile service tax regime where Rule 6(7CA) of Service Tax Rules, 1994 was clearly specified in the related method, the relevant Rules 27 to 35 of the CGST Rules, 2017 for determination of value of supply under GST, are conspicuously silent on the method of valuation to be adopted for levying IGST on such ocean freight services. However, it is important to refer to CORRIGENDUM to Notification No. 8/2017-Integrated tax (Rate) dated 28.06.2017 vide F. No. 334/1/2017-TRU dated 30.06.2017 whereby the following has been inserted:

"4. Where the value of taxable service provided by a person located in non-taxable territory to a person located in non-taxable territory by way of transportation of goods by a vessel from a place outside India up to the customs station of clearance in India is not available with the person liable for paying integrated tax, the same shall be deemed to be 10 % of the CIF value (sum of cost, insurance and freight) of imported goods."

It is evident from the above development that the method of valuation for levying GST on ocean freight has been straight away imported from the erstwhile service tax regime. Therefore, importer should adopt the valuation method as discussed above for discharging GST liability on such transactions.

Now, it is imperative to highlight that, though there are specific rules having clear elaboration on various method of valuations for levying GST on supply of goods or services or both under Rules 27 to 35 of CGST Rules, 2017, the said valuation method for levying GST on ocean freight does not find a place in the said Rules. The above may lead to omission or confusion amongst the importers across the country.

Conclusion

5. It is suggested that GST council should include the said valuation method in the CGST Rules, 2017 itself under "Determination of value of supply" in order to avoid any confusion in the trade. Importers across the country under the spell of any confusion may speculate and act in an arbitrary manner in calculating IGST on such transactions that may lead to disputes in future. Thus, GST council should look into the matter and bring in required consistency on the said method of valuation so that importers across the country can avoid any such valuation blues under GST regime on a future date.

Inspection charges/addition testing charges paid by buyer

12.8-3 Assessee carries out his own inspection and its cost is obviously included in his selling price. However, sometimes, customer carries out additional inspection either himself or through another inspection agency. Sometimes, expenses of such additional inspection/testing are borne by assessee while, in other case, the expenses may be borne by the buyer himself. This inspection is in addition to normal inspection and quality checks of the manufacturer himself. Following points need consideration.

If the inspection charges are to be borne by assessee and goods can be sold only if approved by the inspection agency, the payment is in connection with sale and by reason by sale. It should be includible.

If such testing is a mandatory requirement, it should be includible whether borne by assessee or buyer. This is because there is no sale without such testing.

If assessee has agreed that buyer can reject the goods if not approved by the testing agency, the payment will be 'by reason of sale' and should be includible, whether paid by assessee or buyer.

If the inspection is done by buyer on his own only to satisfy himself about quality of the product, the cost should not be includible, as in such case, the payment made by buyer or expenditure incurred by buyer is not 'on behalf of assessee' but on his own.

If inspection is done at the instance of buyer and charges recovered on actuals, these may not be includible.

This was held as not includible under earlier case law. However, in view of the changed definition, validity of the earlier decisions seem doubtful.

Cost of inspection carried out by buyer on his own is not includible in assessable value on notional basis, as such testing was done by buyer for his own satisfaction - OCP India v. CCE 2003 (156) ELT 378 (CESTAT).

Section 18(a) of the Singapore GST Act specifies that the value of imported goods for the purpose of levy of GST should be the aggregate of the value determined in terms of section 22 of the Singapore Customs Act and the customs duties and other taxes excluding GST levied, if any, on such imports. In the absence of such a reference to the Customs Act, 1962 in the IGST Act, an importer is faced with – Having to negotiate and apply two sets of valuation rules - one prescribed by the Customs Act for the purpose of levy of the Customs duties and another prescribed by the GST Valuation (Determination of the Value of Supply of Goods and Services) Rules, 2016 (hereinafter also referred to as the GST Valuation Rules) for the levy of IGST. The two sets of valuation rules, though similar are not identical. For instance, the GST Valuation Rules similar to the Customs Valuation Rules, do provide for acceptance of transaction value, even if the transaction is between related parties, provided the relationship has not influenced the price. However, unlike the Customs Valuation Rules, the GST Valuation Rules do not provide the method by which the importer can demonstrate that the relationship has not influenced the price and, therefore, the transaction value has to be accepted. Further, one other major difference is that the GST Valuation Rules, unlike the Customs Valuation Rules, do not contain the "Deductive/Sale Minus/Transaction Net Margin (TNMM) method" of valuation. This means that importers who import goods from related parties, especially traders/re-sellers who traditionally rely on the Deductive Method to value their goods or use it to demonstrate that the transaction is at arms' length for the customs valuation would be left in a quandary, as they cannot use this method to arrive at the Value for the purpose of levy of IGST.

There is a lack of clarity on the timing and procedure to pay IGST. Would IGST be levied and collected by the Customs authorities at the time of import together with Customs duties or should it be paid on reverse charge1 basis post-import in the same manner as is applicable to other reverse charge supplies of goods?

Apart from the issues that we have already discussed in the foregoing paragraphs, section 29(1)(b) of the Model Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2016 appears to suggest that input tax credit is available on customs duties paid under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. What does this mean in a GST regime? Does it mean Additional Duties of Customs would continue to be levied under GST regime or does it mean that section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act would be amended to reflect IGST instead of the Additional Duties currently levied? There is a disconnection between the IGST Act and the Customs Tariff Act, both of which attempt to levy IGST on imports. There is not enough information to form an opinion on the questions posed and, as such, we would refrain from making any, suffice to bring out the areas where more information/clarity is required.

The seller also contracts for insurance cover against the buyer's risk of loss of or damage to the goods during the carriage. The buyer should note that under CIF the seller is required to obtain insurance only on minimum cover. Thus, the entire responsibility of all costs till destination is that of the seller and importer shall have cost of product upto his destination port. The Vendor can charge a consolidated amount or can charge separately for different components of the value viz., product sale price, insurance, freight etc, however, the transaction would remain that of CIF and the entire value shall be attributable to the cost of product and no Service Tax shall be applicable on ocean freight. The simple reason being that there is no value attributable to any service for which payment is made by the importer i.e. no service is received by the importer as he is under no obligation to pay for ocean freight to any service provider. Entire value is attributable to the value of goods to be delivered till the destination port and thus, in absence of any element of service therein, no Service Tax is required to be charged / paid on any portion of the value of goods.

Will Service Tax be discharged on full value of Ocean freight

An abatement of 70% is available vide Notification No. 26/2012-Service Tax on the value of services of transport of goods in a vessel. However, the notification provides such abatement is available subject to the condition that CENVAT credit on inputs and capital goods, used for providing the taxable service, has not been taken under the provisions of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Thus, in any case, Service Tax shall be charged / paid on 30% value of such ocean freight.

Will Cenvat Credit be available of the Service Tax paid on Ocean freight?

In case of a manufacturer importer or a provider of taxable services, Cenvat credit of such tax shall be available to him, in case such goods qualify as inputs. However, such tax shall be a cost for an importer trader. It is pertinent to note that no Credit of Swachh Bharat Cess shall be available in all cases. However, Credit of Krishi Kalyan Cess as charged / paid on Ocean freight shall be available to a Service provider against his output liability of Krishi Kalyan Cess. For an importer trader / manufacturer, such charge shall be a cost.

12. It is recognized that the method of valuation provided for in rule 7(3) would normally not be applicable when, as a result of the further processing, the imported goods lose their identity. However there can be instances where, although the identity of the imported goods is lost, the value added by the processing can be determined accurately without unreasonable difficulty. On the other hand, there can also be instances where the imported goods maintain their identity but form such a minor element in the goods sold in the country of importation that the use of this valuation method would be unjustified. In view of the above, each situation of this type must be considered on a case-by-case basis.

Note to rule 8

1. As a general rule, value of imported goods is determined under these rules on the basis of information readily available in India. In order to determine a computed value, however, it may be necessary to examine the costs of producing the goods being valued and other information which has to be obtained from outside India. Furthermore, in most cases, the producer of the goods will be outside the jurisdiction of the proper officer. The use of the computed value method will generally be limited to those cases where the buyer and seller are related, and the producer is prepared to supply to the proper officer the necessary costings and to provide facilities for any subsequent verification which may be necessary.

2. The "cost or value" referred to in clause (a) of rule 8 is to be determined on the basis of information relating to the production of the goods being valued supplied by or on behalf of the producer. It is to be based upon the commercial accounts of the producer, provided that such accounts are consistent with the generally accepted accounting principles applied in the country where the goods are produced.

provision / notification exempting Ocean freight in from Customs duty when Service Tax is levied or vice versa, it would be safe to presume that both levies can be levied on such value of Ocean freight. Having discussed the legal scenario, we shall now discuss the various situations for import and implications of Service Tax under such positions on Ocean freight value.

The position post 01.6.2016, taxability of Ocean freight in case of both import and export can be summarised as under: Clarification in respect of Freight Forwarders

Vide Circular No. 197/7/2016 – Service Tax dated August 12, 2016, it has been clarified that freight forwarder who merely acts as an agent and bears no ownership towards transportation of goods would be called intermediary and their place of provision shall be determined by Rule 9 of Place of Provision Rules, 2012 as its location. However, if the freight forwarder acts as a principal and undertakes risk for transportation of goods and also raises invoice for such transportation, they are not acting as agent but engage themselves for transportation of goods and shall be covered under Rule 10 of Place of Provision Rules, 2012.

Levy of Ocean freight in different import transactions

Situation 1: Import on FOB Value from overseas vendor and ocean freight to domestic Shipping Line

F.O.B ("Free On Board") means that vendor will ship to the origin port and then buyer will take over and have to get the goods picked up from origin port till his destination port. International Chamber of Commerce defines FOB as that the seller delivers the goods on board the vessel nominated by the buyer at the named port of shipment or procures the goods already so delivered. The risk of loss of or damage to the goods passes when the goods are on board the vessel, and the buyer bears all costs from that moment onwards.

Accordingly, the freight, insurance and other costs as required to bring goods to his port shall be liability of Indian Importer and thus, he need to pay for ocean freight and insurance etc. we restrict our discussion to ocean freight and thus, in present scenario, ocean freight is being paid by him to Indian shipping line. In this case, the liability to charge Service Tax shall be on the Indian Shipping line and thus, Indian importer shall pay the requisite tax to the service provider.

Situation 2: Import on FOB Value from overseas vendor and ocean freight to vendor / foreign CHA

Entire situation remains same as provided in Situation 1 above, the only difference being that instead of a domestic Shipping Line, freight is paid to vendor (if he arranges a shipping line on behalf of importer or importer engages a foreign CHA). Under both cases, since the service provider is a non resident, the liability to pay Service Tax shall be shifted to person located in the taxable territory i.e. the importer.

Situation 3: Import on FOB Value from overseas vendor and ocean freight to foreign Shipping Line

Entire situation remains same as provided in Situation 1 above, the only difference being that instead of a domestic Shipping Line, freight is paid to foreign Shipping line. Under this scenario, since the service provider is a non resident, the liability to pay Service Tax shall be shifted to person located in the taxable territory i.e. the importer.

Situation 4: Import on FOB Value from overseas vendor and ocean freight to CHA

Entire situation remains same as provided in Situation 1 above, the only difference being that instead of a domestic Shipping Line, freight is paid to domestic CHA. Under this scenario, if the CHA is charging ocean freight as a pure agent in his invoice and can provide original invoices of Shipping Line in the name of the importer, then the liability shall remain that of the importer under reverse charge. In case, CHA charges Ocean freight otherwise than a pure agent, he shall be liable to pay Service Tax as a provider of service.

Situation 5: Import on CIF Value from overseas vendor

C.I.F ("Cost Insurance and Freight") means that the vendor shall charge value and shall be responsible for all charges upto the destination port. As per International Chamber of Commerce, CIF means that the seller delivers the goods on board the vessel or procures the goods already so delivered. The risk of loss of or damage to the goods passes when the goods are on board the vessel. The seller must contract for and pay the costs and freight necessary to bring the goods to the named port of destination. The seller also contracts for insurance cover against the buyer's risk of loss of or damage to the goods during the carriage. The buyer should note that under CIF the seller is required to obtain insurance only on minimum cover. Thus, the entire responsibility of all costs till destination is that of the seller and importer shall have cost of product upto his destination port.

HEADNOTE: Section  43B  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business disallowance  -  Certain deductions to be allowed only on actual payment  (Customs duty) - Assessment year  2018-19  - During year, assessee-company paid certain customs duty under protest and claimed deduction for same under section 43B - Assessing Officer disallowed same - It was noted that assessee's liability to pay customs duty arose on raising of demand by customs authorities in financial year 2017-18 when assessee imported goods for purpose of selling to its customers in India - Whether since assessee paid customs duty under protest in relevant assessment year and offered to tax amount refunded in pursuance thereof in assessment year 2020-21, impugned addition would lead to double taxation and same was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was engaged in business of marketing, distribution and after sales services of the products manufactured by Keysight Group entities under the Electronic Measurement Group business.

■

During the year under consideration, the assessee paid certain customs duty and while computing the total income, the assessee claimed a deduction under section 43B on account of payment of custom duty.

■

The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

Appellant's liability arises for payment of customs duty on raising of demand by customs authorities in FY 2017-18 as during the year appellant has imported goods for the purpose of selling to its customers in India and as per instructions of CBEC where items are imported from related party the declared import price of said items are required to be certified by Special Valuation Branch (SVB). These instructions mandate that an additional customs charge in the form of Extra Duty Depoists (EDD) of 1% is payable on provisional basis until the investigation is underway. The Appellant has paid 'Extra Duty Deposits (EDD)' in accordance with Circular No. 5/2016 issued by Central Board of Excise and Customs dated 9th February 2016. It comes up that the Appellant has in fact received a favorable order from the SVB wherein the declared price has been accepted and the refunds of the taxes paid was accordingly payable to the Appellant.[Para 5]

■

.It is settled law that once the demand has been quantified, the amount paid towards discharging the liability irrespective of the matter is pending for adjudication at higher level same is an allowable deduction. [Para 6]

■

Once the customs authority order for clearance of goods, then statutory liability of customs duty, is deemed to have incurred by the assessee in such year in which the liability has been paid. Thus, on the basis of the aforesaid discussion, section 43B permits certain deductions only on actual payment of the amounts and same provides a clear departure from the method of accounting followed by an assessee. It allows deduction of statutory liabilities in the year of payment notwithstanding the fact that the liability in respect thereof may have been incurred in another year. More so when assessee has offered to tax in assessment year 2020-21, the amount refunded in pursuance thereof and thus if the impugned addition is sustained it will lead to double taxation. In the light of the aforesaid, the grounds in both the years deserve to be sustained. The appeals of the assessee are allowed. [Para 7]

Whether life insurance service falls under insurance auxiliary services? Yes. With effect from 16-8-2002, insurance auxiliary services in relation to life insurance business are also taxable and, therefore, content of Circular No. B. 11/1/2001, dated 9-7-2001 that only such services are taxable which are in relation to general insurance business and services provided in relation to life insurance are not taxable has become redundant.

Whether services provided by stock and commodity exchange and corresponding clearing and settlement organisation fall under banking and other financial services?

No. The Board has examined the issue with Instruction No. 137/57/2006-CX.4, dated 18-5-2007 and has clarified that services provided by stock and commodity exchanges which provide electronic platform and related services to facilitate and carry on trading of shares, commodity, etc, are not taxable.

Whether dock labour board falls under port services?

Yes. The Government vide its Circular No. B.11/1/2001-TRU, dated 9-7-2001 has clarified that the Dock Labour Board of the port provides service of labour for handling of goods. Accordingly, the Dock Labour Board is liable to pay tax on the labour charges recovered by it.

Whether demurrage charges fall under port services?

Yes. The Government vide its Circular No. B. 11/1/2001-TRU, dated 9-7-2001 has clarified that demurrage charges are recovered by port authority as a rental for storage of goods. The fact that these charges apply only if the goods overstay a prescribed free period, does not detract from their being in the nature of a charge for providing a service in relation to goods. Accordingly, they would form part of taxable value.

Whether a new service introduced from a specific date can be taxed under any other existing category for a period prior to that date?

No. In the case of K.K. Appachan v. CCE [2007] 9 STT 564 (Bang.- CESTAT), the appellant was a licensed labour contractor and he had supplied labourers to a cement factory for rendering assistance in the activity of packing, loading and unloading of cement bags, which was carried out in a mechanised form. He had paid service tax from 16-6-2005 under the category of ‘manpower recruitment and supply agency’, when supply of manpower was also brought into the tax net with effect from that date. The department treated the activity under ‘cargo handling service’ for period 19-8-2002 to 31-3-2004 and levied tax. The Tribunal held that once the department had accepted the fact that the activities carried out by the appellant fell under ‘manpower recruitment and supply agency’ for a later period, it could not levy tax for an earlier period under a different category.

Whether cost of parts or accessories or consumable falls under authorised service station services?

No. In the case of Bajaj Tempo Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (207) ELT 600 (Trib. - Delhi), the Tribunal held that the word ‘accessory’ has a much wider connotation than the word ‘part’ in relation to manufacture of final product. Accessories would not be contained in the final product, yet they would be for use in relation to the manufacture of the final products directly or indrectly. The rules do not provide any catalogue of accessories and, therefore, the meaning of the word ‘accessories’ may be understood in relation to the nature of the final product manufactured and the type of accessories in relation to which it is used.

Whether excavation transportation and feeding of iron ores falls under cargo handling services?

No. In the case of CCE&C v. B K Thakkar [Final Order No. A/1877 (Kol.) of 2007, dated 24-10-2007], the assessee entered into a contract with SAIL for excavation, transportation and feeding of iron ores to the hill top crusher for further processing of iron ores. The department alleged that these services fall under the category of cargo handling services. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that while rendering the above-mentioned activities, there may come incidental activities of loading and unloading of iron, which can’t give the entire contracted activities the character of cargo handling service. The Tribunal held that the activities of the assessee were primarily in the nature of mining activities and the same couldn’t be covered under the cargo handling services.

6.1-5 Tax payable when value is inclusive of GST

Legally, GST is to be indicated separately in tax invoice. However, provision has been made for situations where GST is not shown separately in tax invoice.

If value of supply is inclusive of IGST, CGST, SGST or UTGST, the tax payable will be calculated by back calculations as follows—

Tax amount = [Value inclusive of tax × Tax rate in % of IGST or CGST plus UTGST/SGST]/(100 + sum of applicable tax rates in %). - rule 9 of Valuation Rules - Rule 35 of CGST and SGST Rules, 2017.

Note that the provision applies only the value of supply included GST. The rule does not say that the value is deemed to be inclusive of GST.

For example, when GST is payable under reverse charge, the amount charged by supplier of goods or services cannot be taken as inclusive of GST.

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Custom duty - Assessment year 2007-08 - Whether payment of custom duty for debonding of capital goods increases value of those goods and, therefore, same cannot be allowed as business expenditure - Held, yes [Para 7.2] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: •

During relevant assessment year, the assessee paid certain debonding charges. According to assessee, shifting of capital goods from bonded warehouse on payment of duty did not create any asset and did not lead to benefit of enduring nature as the asset remained the same. Therefore, the expenditure incurred on debonding of capital goods was revenue in nature.

•

The revenue authorities rejected the assessee's claim.

•

On second appeal:

HELD: •

The capital goods placed in the bonded area are subject to restrictions that they cannot be sold and they cannot be removed outside the area for use of self. This encumbrance is removed once the goods are cleared from the bonded area on payment of duty. The result is that the assessee can deal with the goods in any manner it desires including sale thereof.

•

Therefore, payment of custom duty for debonding increases value of the asset and it is required to be added to the costs or written down value, as the case may be. Therefore, this ground raised by assessee is dismissed. [Para 7.2]

The applicant is required to pay interest on the goods imported from E, Turkey, if there is delay in payment of more than 120 days from the date of the invoice, on the value of the goods. [Para 8]

On going through the provisions of section 7 it is found that as per section 7(2)(d), the activities to be treated as supply of goods or supply or services are covered in Schedule II. [Para 8.1] On going through the Schedule II, and comparing the same to the issue in hand, it is found that the foreign buyer has tolerated the act of receiving payment after a lapse of a period of 120 days from the date of the invoice in respect of the goods supplied by them to the applicant for which interest is to be paid by the applicant. Therefore, the aforementioned act will be covered under the Supply of Services under Entry No. 5(e) of the aforementioned Schedule II which reads as '(e) agreeing to the obligation to refrain from an act, or to tolerate an act or a situation, or to do an act'. However, since the payment of interest made by the applicant to the foreign buyer is connected to the goods imported by them and is with regard to the late payment of the value of goods imported by them from the foreign buyer, it is absolutely necessary to refer to section 15 which covers the valuation aspect in respect of supply of goods and services. [Para 8.2]

Section 15(2) pertains to all the things that shall be included in the value of supply. On going through the said sub-section, it is found that as per section 15(2)(d), value of supply also includes 'interest or late fee or penalty for delayed payment of any consideration for any supply.' Therefore, the payment of interest by the applicant will be covered under the supply of services under Entry No. 5(2)(e) of Schedule II and is liable to GST in view of the provisions of section 15(2)(d). [Para 8.3]

The interest paid by the applicant for delay in payment of the amount/value of the imported goods (paid after a lapse of a period of 120 days from the date of the invoice) is included as a part of the value of the said goods as per the provisions of section 15(2)(d). In view of the above, it is concluded that the rate of GST payable on the aforementioned interest will be the same as that of the IGST applicable on the aforementioned goods. [Para 8.4]

Conclusion and parting remarks

While the issuance of said Circular is undoubtedly a step forward with the Board specifically taking cognizance and resolving the issues where payment is made vide TR-06 challan, the Circular has also parallelly opened a Pandora's box and aggravated the concerns of assessees in the aforementioned scenarios wherein no similar procedure has been prescribed to facilitate the availment of ITC legally accrued to such assessees. Such ambiguity continues to cause further confusion and unnecessary litigations among assessees. The additional issue of the jurisdictional customs officers refusing to amend the BOEs despite repeated requests of the importers so as to enable the flow of ITC also adds to the problem. Therefore, even the directions given in the present Circular for reassessment of the BOEs may not achieve the desired results. Additionally, the issue still remains open as to whether an assessee can get their BoEs re-assessed in respect of IGST already paid previously through TR-06 Challan in order to avail ITC.

To conclude, the industry expects the Board to further prescribe similar mechanism and procedure to enable the assessees to avail ITC which are legally accruing to them in the aforementioned scenarios, which is otherwise disallowed to them due to mere procedural ambiguities. Further, the industries may also file a suitable representation before the Government of India/Board, explaining such practical difficulties in the availment of ITC basis a standalone TR-06 Challan and how the absence of such mechanism/procedure as issued under the Circular continues to result in redundancy of efforts, increased ambiguities and the requirement to undertake undue compliances.

OT charges/penalties were exigible under ‘Storage and Warehousing services’. On appeal : HELD: From the case records, it was found that the assessee had collected various charges from importers/exporters including passengers for keeping the cargo in transit safely, pending export or customs clearance for home consumption. In holding that keeping safe custody of cargo in transit, pending clearance by the customs would constitute an activity exigible under the above entry, the lower authorities had relied on Circulars of the CBEC which clarified that storage and warehousing service provided by, inter alia, Airport Authority is covered by the entry. The entry cargo handling service was clarified by the CBEC as not covering export cargo and passenger baggage. The clarification was not to the effect that all activities relating to export cargo and passenger baggage were also excluded from levy under other entries. The finding of the Commissioner, that the exceptions provided under cargo handling services with regard to passenger baggage and export cargo could not be claimed under storage and warehousing services, was to be agreed with. [Para 9.2]

Demurrage or wharfage charges were collected, respectively, in relation to clearance of import/export cargo beyond five days and 24 hours. As found by the original authority, these were higher charges for continued storage of cargo collected by the assessee from members of the trade. These were part of the taxable value collected towards storage and warehouse charges. [Para 9.3]

As regards the abandoned cargo, those accrued to the assessee towards storage and warehousing of cargo, which were not taken delivery of by the importer. The procedure for auctioning abandoned cargo and the sharing of the proceeds is prescribed by the Ministry of Finance. These instructions also make it clear that the assessee would receive amounts towards the service of storage and warehousing of cargo under this head. However, the services were not rendered to any person in the case of the abandoned cargo. Therefore, demand under this head was not sustainable. [Para 9.4]

As regards the destination charges, it was found that the assessee had collected the documents representing the consignments brought by Air India and Blue Dart and hand over these to the respective consignees. In cases where the assessee merely collected and handed over the documents to the respective consignees, destination charges would not form part of taxable value under storage and warehousing. [Para 9.5]

As regards the OT charges/penalties, the lower authorities had not given a finding as to the nature and purpose of these penalties but had presumed that these were collected for violations on the part of their clients in relation to storage and warehousing services. The Commissioner (Appeals) did not find this item to be taxable under storage and warehousing. In the absence of a finding as to how that amount was taxable towards any service rendered by the assessee, it was difficult to accept the stand of the revenue in this regard. The assessee had also not explained the nature and purpose of collecting these charges. This matter would be decided after hearing the party afresh. [Para 9.6]

There was considerable merit in the assessee’s submission that there was no suppression of facts, etc. to warrant invocation of larger period. From the orders impugned, one did not find a reliable finding by the authorities that the assessee, a State PSU, had resorted to suppression of the facts to evade appropriate service tax amount. Considering the nature of the activities involved, the Commissioner could not have found with certainty that the assessee had deliberately mis-classified the activities undertaken by it under the head ‘Cargo handling services’ instead of ‘Storage and warehousing services’. Therefore, the authorities could not have validly invoked extended period and imposed penalties. The penal liability of the assessee required reconsideration in the light of section 80. [Para 9.7]

Exceptions where investigations under SVB not required:

b.

Wherever the investigation by SVBs are not required, Customs house shall issue a reference number to the importer and the risk management division to indicate that the transaction has been analyzed from the viewpoint of SVB enquiries and it has been decided not to refer the same for the investigation.

Locations and Jurisdiction of SVB Units:

The Special Valuation Branches are currently functional at following Customs location houses i.e., Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi, Mumbai. Further, the jurisdiction of SVB would entirely be dependent on the corporate or registered office of the importer, whichever is nearby and convenient to the importer.

The importer is given free hand to choose which SVB he wants to approach for the cases which require investigation by the SVB. Once a particular import transaction has triggered investigation at one SVB, then the same needs to be communicated by the customs houses to other SVBs as well for the better compliance of the process involved.

Procedure for investigation under SVB :

Finalization of Assessment :

Upon receipt of Investigation report from the Special Valuation branch, there could be two scenarios which could affect the assessment -

a.

Declared Value is found confirming to Rule 3: Where the declared value as per Bill of Entry has been found confirming to the relevant rule of the CVR,2007 - the provisional assessment done by the customs houses shall be considered the final assessment and accordingly it must be finalized.

b.

Declared Value is found not confirming to Rule 3: Where the declared value as per Bill of Entry is found to be influenced by the relationship or such case as may be applicable, the proper office of the customs house shall issue a show cause notice to the importer within 15 days of the receipt of the Investigation Report (IR) from the Special Valuation Branch (SVB).

Wherever the imports have been cleared through multiple locations, jurisdictional commissioner shall after consulting with other locations, make a proposal for appointment of common adjudicating authority for the matter and after providing enough opportunity to the importer, pass a combined order quantifying the extent of influence on the declared transaction value.

Concept of Extra Duty Deposit/Revenue Deposit :

As per Circular No. 01/98 dated 1-1-1988, there was a duty called extra duty deposit which was applicable in cases where the documents sought for are not provided to the relevant authorities failing for which the higher extra duty deposit shall be leviable. However, in the circular issued in 2016, board has reviewed the levy and has clarified that no security in form of extra duty deposit shall be obtained from the importers, but if the importer fails to provide the information within 60 days of such requisition, security deposit at a higher rate of 5% shall be imposed by the commissioner which shall be valid for the period of 3 months.

Explanation 2.—Where an assessee receives any advance payment from the buyer against delivery of any excisable goods, no notional interest on such advance shall be added to the value unless the Central Excise Officer has evidence to the effect that the advance received has influenced the fixation of the price of the goods by way of charging a lesser price from or by offering a special discount to the buyer who has made the advance deposit.

Illustration 1.—X, an assessee, sells his goods to Y against full advance payment at Rs. 100 per piece. However, X also sells such goods to Z without any advance payment at the same price of Rs. 100 per piece. No notional interest on the advance received by X is includible in the transaction value.

Illustration 2.—A, an assessee, manufactures and supplies certain goods as per design and specification furnished by B at a price of Rs. 10 lakhs A takes 50% of the price as advance against these goods and there is no sale of such goods to any other buyer. There is no evidence available with the Central Excise Officer that the notional interest on such advance has resulted in lowering of the prices. Thus, no notional interest on the advance received shall be added to the transaction value.

Where in case of assessee-corporation which had been established for distribution of liquor within State of Karnataka by purchase and sale of liquor from various manufacturers and distilleries, liquor had not been lifted within 90 days, demurrage charges were levied by supplier, the Tribunal held that the assessee was not liable to pay service tax on charges collected as ‘storage charges’ under the category of ‘Storage and warehousing services’. [Karnataka State Beverages Corpn. Ltd. v. CST [2007] 11 STT 363 (Bang. - CESTAT)]

Section 65(105)(zzi) - Taxable service - Technical inspection and certification service - Technical testing and certification of energy meters

Where assessee was engaged in production and distribution of electricity and it was required to carry out technical testing and certification of energy meters installed at premises of customers in terms of statutory requirement, the Tribunal held that the same could not be liable to service tax under category of ‘testing and certification service’ in view of the Board’s Circular No. 89/2006/ST, dated December 18, 2006. [Kerala State Electricity Board (T.M.R. Division) v. CCE [2007] 11 STT 361 (Bang. - CESTAT)]

Section 67(2) - Valuation of taxable services for charging service tax - When no tax is separately collected from client

Section 67(2) inserted on September 10, 2002, only clarifies general principle that when no tax is separately collected from client, gross amount collected is inclusive of tax, and therefore, it is applicable to earlier period also. [GEM Star Enterprises (P.) Ltd. v. CCE&C [2007] 11 STT 335 (Bang. - CESTAT)]

Section 73, read with section 86, of the Finance Act, 1994 - Recovery of service tax not levied or paid or short-levied or short-paid or erroneously refunded

Where for same activity a show-cause notice was issued in November, 2001 and adjudicated by an order dated January 22, 2003, confirming demand of service tax, the Tribunal held that once there was knowledge with department about activities of the applicants, suppression could not continue thereafter and adjudicating notices issued in March, 2003 and November, 2004 were held barred by limitation. [Ajinkyatara Sahakari Krishi Audyogik OTVS Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 11 STT 472 (Mum . - CESTAT)]

Amendment of section 44B.

15. In section 44B of the Income-tax Act, after sub-section (2), the following Explanation shall be inserted and shall be deemed to have been inserted with effect from the 1st day of April, 1976, namely:—

"Explanation .—For the purposes of this sub-section, the amount referred to in clause (i) or clause (ii) shall include the amount paid or payable or received or deemed to be received, as the case may be, by way of demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature.".

In the current tax environment, it is not uncommon for assessments to remain provisional for very long periods, sometimes even spanning several years. These delays not only stifle the growth of businesses but also strain their financial resources. Businesses face mounting costs, with execution of bank guarantees/bonds, payments of higher duties on continuing provisional assessments and delay in clearance of imported goods. The framework governing these assessments has evolved over the years but often fell short in practice, especially when it comes to finalisation in a time bound manner.

The problem has been especially acute when it comes to finalisation of assessments post determination of values by Special Valuation Branch (SVB). Currently, Circular No. 05/2016-Customs dated 09.02.2016 governs the procedure for SVB proceedings and requires the assessments to be kept provisional pending investigation by the SVB. The Circular stipulates a timeframe of 60 days for the importers/exporters to submit the relevant information. Thereafter, a period of two months (further extendable by two more months) is provided for completion of investigations from the date of receipt of information. However, this period can be extended further at the discretion of Chief Commissioner.

Similar to the SVB proceedings, long delays have also been seen in cases of finalisation of provisional assessments for grant of Project Import benefits. While Circular 22/2011-Customs dated 04.05.2011 provides that finalization of assessments under Project imports should be completed within a period of 60 days from the date of submission of documents by the importer, however this period is also extendable by the by the jurisdictional Commissioner of Customs.

The consequence is that sometimes the assessments are kept provisional and pending for years all together. In fact, even after the enforcement of the Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2018, assessments are rarely finalised in a time bound manner.

Recognizing these issues, the recent amendment proposed in Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1962 via the Finance Bill, 2025 is a promising development and a welcome change.

I. Key changes proposed to Section 18 of Customs Act, 1962.

The proposed sub-section (1B) to Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1962 aims to provide a definite time limit of two years, extendable by one year (at the discretion of the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs) for finalization of provisional assessments. The Section provides that the proper officer shall finalize the assessment within two years from the date of such provisional assessment. For cases that are currently pending, the time limit is proposed to be calculated from the date of assent of the Finance Bill, 2025. The application of this proposed amendment to pending assessments will ensure that existing cases are also governed by the new timelines, promoting efficiency in the resolution of outstanding assessments.

Sub-section (1C) is also aimed at outlining specific reasons on which the two-year time limit for finalizing provisional assessments may be suspended. These include cases (a) where information is sought from an authority outside India through legal processes; (b) where assessments have been kept on hold for want of decision from the higher courts or an Appellant Tribunal; (c) where an interim order of stay has been issued by the Appellate Tribunal or higher courts; (d) where the Board has issued a specified direction or order to keep a matter pending; or (e) where an importer or exporter has an application pending before the Settlement Commission or the Interim Board.

In such cases, it is mandatory for the proper officer to inform the concerned importer/exporter about the reasons for non-finalisation of provisional assessments. It is proposed that the two-year time limit will commence from the date when the reason for delay ceases to exist and not from the date of provisional assessment/the date of assent of Finance Bill, 2025. This flexibility is perhaps intended to accommodate exceptional circumstances that may prevent timely assessments, thereby ensuring that legitimate trade activities are not unduly hindered.

II. Concern that remains unresolved

While the proposed amendment to Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1962 provides much-needed certainty and transparency to importers/exporters, there is one significant concern that remains unresolved.

There is lack of clarity on the consequences if assessments are not finalized within the proposed timeframe. While the use of word 'shall' does indicate a mandatory requirement to finalise assessments within the prescribed timeframe, however the answer to this question may not be as simple as it seems. In the past, the courts have held that it is necessary to analyse the legislative purpose of a provision and potential consequences of non-compliance1. It has been held that 'shall' can be interpreted both literally (implying a mandatory requirement), or more liberally (indicating a directory nature) depending on the legislative intent and context.2

SVB ensures that all connected payments are adequately disclosed and incorporated into the valuation. 6. Circumstances Exempt from SVB Investigations:

While SVB investigations are essential for ensuring accurate customs valuation, there are certain instances where such investigations are unnecessary, particularly when the revenue implications are negligible. Key exemptions include:

Samples and Prototypes: Imports involving samples or prototypes from related suppliers, which hold minimal commercial value, are exempt from SVB investigations.

Imports with Full Duty Exemption: Where the imported goods are fully exempt from customs duties or the applicable duty rate is nil, SVB investigations are not required, as there is no revenue impact.

Low-Value Imports: Transactions below Rs. 1 lakh, provided the cumulative value of such transactions does not exceed Rs. 25 lakhs in a financial year, are exempt from SVB scrutiny, ensuring that small-scale imports are not unnecessarily delayed.

7. Jurisdictional Framework of SVBs:

Currently, SVBs operate out of five key customs locations across India:

Bengaluru

Chennai

Kolkata

Delhi

Mumbai

The jurisdiction of an SVB is typically determined by the location of the importer's corporate or registered office.

8. Reform of Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) Provisions:

The earlier SVB regime was heavily criticized for its imposition of EDD—1% of the declared assessable value—which could be escalated to 5% in cases of non-compliance with document submission timelines. This was widely regarded as an excessive burden on trade. In response to industry representations, the government eliminated the requirement for EDD in Circular No. 05/2016.

However, under the revised regime, if an importer fails to submit the requisite documentation within 60 days, the customs authorities may impose a security deposit of 5%, valid for an initial period of three months. This deposit can be furnished in the form of either a cash payment or a bank guarantee, providing flexibility to the importer while ensuring compliance with customs requirements.

9. Conclusion:

The SVB's investigatory powers are pivotal in safeguarding the integrity of the customs valuation process, particularly in complex related-party transactions where the declared value may be subject to manipulation. The intricate interplay between contractual terms, such as royalties, and the customs valuation process necessitates careful oversight by SVBs to prevent undervaluation. Importers, for their part, can mitigate the time and cost implications of SVB investigations by ensuring full compliance with documentation requirements and maintaining transparency in their transactional relationships.

SERVICE TAX - WORKS CONTRACT PROJECTS UNDER CONSORTIUMS 7. We are executing EPC project for a client under Consortium agreement with a Foreign Vendor. Imported supplies are to be made by Foreign Consortium partner under FOB basis and Ocean freight, C & F Agent commission, inland transport expenses will be borne and paid by us. Taxes & Duties such as Custom duty, CVD, SAD etc. will be borne and paid by ultimate client. The amount paid towards Ocean freight, C & F Agent commission, inland transport expenses will be claimed by us from the ultimate client.

Whether all amount claimed for aforesaid expenses will subject to service tax ? If yes, on which amount, service tax would be calculated ?

Can client take CENVAT credit of service tax claimed, if any on the aforesaid transaction?

The query is replied in following parts :

Joint Venture : In this case, you and your consortium partner appear to be taking joint responsibility (supply of goods by foreign partner, their clearance and installation by you) and, therefore, there appears to come into existence a 'Joint Venture'.

Works contract : The EPC contract appear to be 'works contract' and hence, valuation of taxable services will be done as per Rule 2A of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006.

Contract price : It appears that irrespective of manner of payment (whether as reimbursement or otherwise), all payments made by Indian customer are for EPC/works contract and would therefore, form part of contract price. In short, contract price = Price as per contract = All inclusive except tax on contract price. Hence, Contract price would cover all payments made by service recipient (viz. Indian client) and would also cover all expenses and costs that are charged from ultimate customer.

Valuation on actual basis : If valuation on actual basis under rule 2A(i) is adopted, only service portion would be liable to service tax and sale value (FOR value or market value) of goods would be allowed as deduction.

Valuation on deemed basis : If valuation on deemed basis under rule 2A(ii), 40% of contract price would be adopted as value of services.

Cenvat Credit : Credit may be availed by client as per Rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, only if this does not relate to construction of immovable property. However, set up of plant and machinery (except immovable base) is eligible for credit.

2.2 Any activity relating to business is ‘input service’ - There is no qualification to the word ‘activities’. There is no restriction that activities relating to business should be relating to only main activities or essential activities. All activities relating to business fall within the definition of ‘input service’.

2.3 Meaning of ‘such as’ - The expression ‘such as’ is purely illustrative ‘such as’ means ‘for example’ or ‘of a kind that’ (Concise Oxford Dictionary), ‘for example’ (Chambers Dictionary).

2.4 ‘Valuation’ and ‘Cenvat credit’ are independent of each other - The two issues, namely, valuation and Cenvat credit are independent of each other and have no relevance to each other. The submission of the revenue that Cenvat credit cannot be allowed for services if value thereof does not form part of value subjected to excise duty is clearly against the fundamental concept laid down by the Supreme Court in All India Federation of Tax Practitioners and the OECD guidelines.

There is an additional reason for holding that Cenvat credit is admissible on services even if the value thereof is not part of value subjected to duty. This is because the interpretation of the expression ‘input services’ cannot fluctuate with the change in the definition of ‘value’ in section 4 of the Central Excise Act and cannot vary depending on whether goods are levied to duty under section 4A of the Central Excise Act or tariff value under section 3(2) of the Central Excise Act or the product attracts specific rate of duty.

2.5 If cost included in assessable value, Cenvat credit is available - It was observed that ‘question of denial of Cenvat credit does not arise if cost of (outward) freight is included in the transaction value’.

Thus, if a cost is included in assessable value, its Cenvat credit will be certainly eligible. [However, just because it is not included, it will still be eligible if it is in relation to business of assessee].

2.6 Definition of ‘input service’ is not confined to ‘manufacture’ but has to be interpreted on basis of requirements of business - The definition of ‘input service’ has to be interpreted in the light of the requirements of business and cannot be read restrictively so as to confine only up to the factory or only up to depot of manufacturers.

2.7 Outward freight eligible for Cenvat credit - Finally, the Tribunal concluded that outward freight is ‘input service’ even if its cost is not included in assessable value of goods [If outward freight is not included in assessable value, the assessee should be very careful while taking Cenvat credit since dispute regarding assessable value may arise].

However, the decision of three member Bench goes much beyond the issue of ‘outward freight’ and, in effect, it has been held that any service in relation to business of the assessee is its input service.

Clarity on GST applicability on permanent transfer/assignment of leasehold rights The issue of taxing the permanent transfer of leasehold rights under the GST regime has generated considerable debate and uncertainty. Although the matter is currently sub-judice, issuing a circular to clarify the taxability would benefit all stakeholders and also clarify the taxability of the permanent transfer of leasehold rights, which would significantly benefit businesses by reducing uncertainty and litigation. By aligning it with the tax treatment of the sale of immovable property, the government can ensure a more consistent and predictable tax environment for stakeholders.

60. GST on Corporate Guarantee

Taxation of corporate guarantee has been a matter of litigation since the inception of GST. Specifically, when a holding company provides a corporate guarantee for its subsidiary company, it is argued that such activity is merely a shareholder's activity and is not a service provided by the holding company.

However, with effect from 26-10-2023, a new sub-rule (2) has been inserted11 to Rule 28 of the CGST Rules to provide a specific manner of valuation of corporate guarantee when a person provides corporate guarantee to any banking company or financial institution on behalf of its related person. Notably, the said provision has an overriding effect on the existing methods of valuation prescribed under Rule 28. After this insertion, the taxability of corporate guarantee has also been clarified by the CBIC by issuing a detailed Circular No. 204/16/2023-GST, dated 27-10-2023.

Further, the involvement of the service element in extending corporate guarantee is still a subject matter of litigation. Recently, the Punjab and Haryana High Court issued12 notices to the Revenue and granted interim relief by putting a stay on part of the Circular. The Court also directed the authority to decide the case without being influenced by the impugned clarification.

Hence, it is recommended that suitable amendments must be made to the law to clarify the applicability of the given provision.

(Read more : Valuation as per CGST Rules on Taxmann.com/Practice)

61. Allowing utilisation of credit ledger balance for reverse charge payments

Under the GST law, there are certain provisions, which are resulting in cash blockages without yielding any incremental revenue for the Government. For instance, on the import of services, a recipient of services is liable to discharge GST liability in cash under a reverse charge mechanism, which will then be available to him as ITC. The mandatory payment in cash leads to cash blockage.

The Government should consider allowing taxpayers to use their ITC balance of GST for payment of tax under the reverse charge mechanism. The ability to use ITC balance to discharge the RCM liability would not only address the cash flow issues but also streamline the tax administration process, making it more business-friendly without compromising the tax revenues for the Government.

(Read more : Reverse Charge under GST and Electronic Credit Ledger under GST on Taxmann.com/Practice)

62. Whether to compute interest on Gross or Net tax amount after utilising ITC?

Under the GST laws, the interest is typically calculated on the amount of tax payable, for the period of delay in filing the periodical return. According to Section 50 of the CGST Act, 2017 if a registered person fails to pay tax by the due date, it shall be liable to pay interest at a prescribed rate of 18 percent.

There was uncertainty about whether interest should be calculated on the total tax owed (i.e., the gross amount of tax payable) or just the net amount after adjusting available input tax credits in the electronic credit ledger for that period.

To address this, the GST Council, during its 31st meeting, recommended that interest should only be due on a net basis, i.e. tax paid in cash through the electronic cash ledger. In this regard, relevant amendments were retrospectively notified from the inception of GST in order to prevent potential legal issues.

However, a recent ruling by Patna High Court13 has resurfaced this issue and held that interest charges automatically apply to delayed return filings, regardless of whether payments are made through the Electronic Credit or Cash Ledger. The Court observed that the input tax credit and the resultant payment of tax from the Electronic Credit Ledger occurs only when a return is furnished. If there is a delay in furnishing of returns, then there is a delay in the input tax credit coming into the Electronic Credit Ledger and a resultant payment being made to the Government as tax is belated, leading to a levy of interest.
